title: A share and an option are different
teach: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. An option is a contract with a deadline. Buying an option does not mean you already own the shares. An ETF is a basket of investments traded like a stock.
example: Buying one share for $40 costs $40. Buying a standard stock option quoted at $2 normally costs $200 because it represents 100 shares. These are different purchases.
watch: An option buyer can lose the entire amount paid. Practice with pretend money first.

questions.prompt: Which purchase normally costs $200?
questions.explanation: Buying one share for $40 costs $40. Buying a standard stock option quoted at $2 normally costs $200 because it represents 100 shares. These are different purchases. An option buyer can lose the entire amount paid. Practice with pretend money first.

workshop.goal: Explain what you own, read an option quote, and calculate what one contract costs.

steps.title: Start with the thing you are buying
steps.explain: A share is ownership. If you buy one share of a company, you own a small part of it. A purchased option is a contract giving you a particular right for a limited time. Buying the contract does not put the shares into your account.
steps.example: One share at $40 costs $40. One standard option quoted at $2 costs $200 before fees. The $2 is a price per share covered by the contract, not the price for the whole contract.

steps.title: Read the contract like a product label
steps.explain: The ticker tells you the investment. Call or put tells you the right. Strike tells you the agreed share price. Expiration tells you the deadline. Premium is the price of the contract, quoted per share. You need all five pieces to know what you are buying.
steps.example: XYZ $50 call, expiring June 18, quoted at $2: XYZ is the investment, call is the right to buy, $50 is the strike, June 18 is expiration, and $2 is the premium. This is a made-up teaching contract.

steps.title: Separate the purchase from the right
steps.explain: For a standard 100-share call, paying $200 buys the contract. It does not buy 100 shares for $200. Using the right to buy shares is called exercising and requires paying the strike price for those shares.
steps.example: Exercising that $50 call normally requires $5,000 to purchase 100 shares. That is separate from the $200 already paid for the option.

steps.title: Know how the purchase can end
steps.explain: An option buyer can sell the contract to close it before expiration, if a buyer is available. Exercising is different from selling the option. If the contract expires worthless, the buyer loses the entire premium paid, plus costs.
steps.example: Buy one contract for $200 and later sell it for $250: the difference is $50 before fees. If it becomes worthless instead, the loss is $200 before fees. These are examples, not predictions.

workshop.mistake: The $50 strike is not a $50 option price. Do not multiply the strike to calculate what buying the option costs. Use the premium and the contract multiplier.

challenge.prompt: A standard option is quoted at $1.25. You buy two contracts. What do you pay before fees?
challenge.explanation: $1.25 × 100 × 2 = $250. The 100 converts the per-share quote to one standard contract. The 2 is the number of contracts. Check the multiplier because adjusted contracts can differ.

title: Build a practice routine
teach: Learning is a skill, not a race to make money. Start with a question, write a prediction, then check what happened. Paper trading uses pretend money. Real orders can behave differently.
example: Before a practice trade, write: I think price may rise because it held a previous low. I will leave if my written exit condition happens. Afterward, compare the result to the plan.
watch: A winning practice trade can still be a poorly planned trade. Judge the process as well as the result.

questions.prompt: Which is the better learning habit?
choices: Record the reason and review the outcome
questions.explanation: Before a practice trade, write: I think price may rise because it held a previous low. I will leave if my written exit condition happens. Afterward, compare the result to the plan. A winning practice trade can still be a poorly planned trade. Judge the process as well as the result.

workshop.goal: Write a testable paper-trade plan and judge the decision separately from its outcome.

steps.title: Choose one skill to practice
steps.explain: Do not try to learn contract selection, chart patterns and fast execution all at once. Pick a specific skill, such as calculating contract cost or recognizing a completed candle. Paper trading is a practice environment using simulated money.
steps.example: Today’s task: before every pretend purchase, calculate its total premium cost. Record your calculation before looking at the platform total.

steps.title: Write the observation, then the decision
steps.explain: An observation describes what you can see. A prediction describes what you think may happen. Keep them separate so you can later check whether the decision followed the evidence.
steps.example: Observation: two completed candles stayed above $50. Prediction: buyers may defend $50 again. Neither sentence proves that the next candle will rise.

steps.title: Make the plan specific enough to check
steps.explain: Before a paper entry, record the contract, entry price, quantity, reason, exit condition and maximum money exposed. “Leave if it looks bad” cannot be tested consistently. These example rules are exercises, not recommended trading settings.
steps.example: Practice example: one contract bought at $2.00; close the simulated position if its bid reaches $1.80 or at the chosen practice end time. A $1.80 sale would lose $20 before fees. An actual exit can be worse if the price jumps or the order cannot fill.

steps.title: Review the process before the score
steps.explain: Compare the actions with the plan. A gain does not prove a good process, and a loss does not prove that a rule is useless. Keep losing examples so you can identify repeated mistakes.
steps.example: If the plan said one contract but you bought five and made money, the sizing decision still broke the plan. Record both facts. Paper fills also do not prove the same order would fill in a real account.

workshop.mistake: Do not change the explanation after you know the outcome. Write what you saw and intended before revealing the next candle.

challenge.prompt: Your paper plan allowed one contract. You bought four and made $80. What should your review say?

Delete the trade because it was not planned
challenge.explanation: Keep the result and the mistake. The gain is real within the simulation, but it does not validate buying four contracts. Review why the quantity changed before repeating the exercise.

title: Calls: the right to buy
teach: A call gives its buyer the right to buy shares at a stated price, called the strike, by the contract deadline. The expiration is that deadline. Buying a call often expresses a rising-price view, but a rising stock does not guarantee a profitable call.
example: A $50 call lets its holder buy at $50 under the contract terms. If the stock is $54 at expiration, the call has $4 per share of intrinsic value. If you paid $5, that is still a loss before costs.
watch: The strike is not the price you pay for the option. The premium is.

questions.prompt: What is the strike?
choices: The contract’s stated share purchase price
questions.explanation: A $50 call lets its holder buy at $50 under the contract terms. If the stock is $54 at expiration, the call has $4 per share of intrinsic value. If you paid $5, that is still a loss before costs. The strike is not the price you pay for the option. The premium is.

workshop.goal: Distinguish a call’s strike, premium and expiration value, then calculate a simple result.

steps.title: Understand the right
steps.explain: A purchased call gives its holder the right to buy the underlying shares at the strike under the contract’s terms. A standard equity call usually covers 100 shares. Buying a call does not force the stock to rise.
steps.example: A $50 call gives a right to buy at $50. The $50 is the share price in the agreement, not the amount paid for the call.

steps.title: Pay attention to the price of that right
steps.explain: The premium is what you pay for the option. A call can become more useful as the stock rises, yet still leave you with a loss if you paid too much relative to what you receive when you exit.
steps.example: One call quoted at $3 costs $300 before fees. Selling that same contract at $2.50 returns $250, a $50 loss before fees, even if the stock rose slightly.

steps.title: Work through expiration
steps.explain: At expiration, the call’s intrinsic value per share is the stock price minus the strike, with a minimum of zero. Intrinsic value means the value of the right itself at that point. Subtract the premium paid to find the simplified expiration result.
steps.example: Stock $54, strike $50: intrinsic value $4. Pay $3 originally and the simplified result is ($4 − $3) × 100 = $100 before fees. Pay $5 instead and it is a $100 loss.

steps.title: Do not confuse expiration math with today’s sale price
steps.explain: Before expiration, the option can also have value from time remaining and uncertainty about future prices. Use an actual option quote to estimate a sale, not just the stock price minus strike. Exercising involves separate funding and broker rules.
steps.example: If the stock is $51, a $50 call might be quoted above $1 before expiration. You cannot calculate its exact bid from those two stock prices alone.

workshop.mistake: “The stock went up” and “my call made money” are different statements. Compare the option purchase and sale prices, including costs.

challenge.prompt: At expiration, a $60 call has a stock price of $64. You paid a $5 premium for one standard contract. What is the simplified result before fees?
challenge.explanation: Intrinsic value is $64 − $60 = $4 per share, or $400 per contract. You paid $500, so the result is a $100 loss. The call has value, but not enough to recover its cost.

title: Puts: the right to sell
teach: A put gives its buyer the right to sell shares at the strike by expiration. A purchased put often expresses a falling-price view. Buying a put is different from selling shares short.
example: A $50 put has $4 per share of intrinsic value when the stock is $46 at expiration. If its premium was $2, its expiration value exceeds that premium by $2 per share before costs.
watch: Selling a put to open a position creates an obligation. That is not the same as buying a put.

questions.prompt: Which contract gives its buyer the right to sell at the strike?
questions.explanation: A $50 put has $4 per share of intrinsic value when the stock is $46 at expiration. If its premium was $2, its expiration value exceeds that premium by $2 per share before costs. Selling a put to open a position creates an obligation. That is not the same as buying a put.

workshop.goal: Explain a purchased put and calculate its result without confusing it with selling a put.

steps.title: Understand what the put lets you do
steps.explain: A put gives its buyer the right to sell the underlying shares at the strike under the contract’s terms. A purchased put often benefits from a falling stock price, but direction alone does not guarantee a profit.
steps.example: If the market price is $46, the right to sell at $50 has value. The put’s strike is $50, regardless of the premium you paid.

steps.title: Calculate the purchase cost
steps.explain: Use the option premium, multiplier and quantity. A standard equity put usually uses 100 shares, just as a standard call does. The word put does not change this cost calculation.
steps.example: One put quoted at $2 costs $200 before fees. Two cost $400. This buys contracts, not a short position in 200 shares.

steps.title: Calculate the simplified expiration result
steps.explain: At expiration, a put’s intrinsic value per share is strike minus stock price, with a minimum of zero. Subtract what you paid, then multiply by 100 for a standard contract.
steps.example: Strike $50, stock $46, premium paid $2: ($50 − $46 − $2) × 100 = $200 before fees. If the stock is $49 instead, the result is ($1 − $2) × 100 = a $100 loss.

steps.title: Separate closing from opening
steps.explain: Selling a put that you already bought closes that long position. Selling a put to open a new short position is different: it creates an obligation if assigned. The lessons here are not permission to sell uncovered options.
steps.example: Buy one put at $2 and sell that same one at $2.60: you have closed it for $60 before fees. You did not open a new short put merely because the closing button says Sell.

workshop.mistake: Calls and puts are types of contracts. Buy and sell are actions. A put position can start with a Buy and end with a Sell.

You closed it for $0.70 before fees
challenge.explanation: The price difference is $0.70 per share. $0.70 × 100 = $70 before fees. Selling the contract you own closes the position.

title: Read the contract before the chart
teach: Check the ticker, call or put, strike, expiration, premium and multiplier. A standard equity option usually represents 100 shares. Adjusted contracts can differ, so check rather than assume.
example: Two standard contracts at $1.80 cost 2 × $1.80 × 100 = $360 before fees. Buying twice as many contracts doubles the money exposed to the same price move.
watch: A cheap-looking quote can still represent a large total cost.

questions.prompt: Three standard contracts at $2 cost how much before fees?
questions.explanation: Two standard contracts at $1.80 cost 2 × $1.80 × 100 = $360 before fees. Buying twice as many contracts doubles the money exposed to the same price move. A cheap-looking quote can still represent a large total cost.

workshop.goal: Read an option ticket and calculate the total purchase before pressing Buy.

steps.title: Identify the exact product
steps.explain: A ticker alone is not a contract. The same stock can have many strikes, expiration dates and both calls and puts. Read those fields together. Otherwise you can buy a different exposure from the one you intended.
steps.example: XYZ June 18 $50 call and XYZ June 18 $50 put share a ticker and strike, but give different rights. A July contract also has a different deadline.

steps.title: Turn the quote into dollars
steps.explain: The premium is quoted per share. Multiply it by the contract multiplier and quantity to find the purchase cost. A standard equity contract normally uses 100. Adjusted contracts can differ, so verify the contract details.
steps.example: Two standard contracts at $1.80 cost $1.80 × 100 × 2 = $360 before fees. A $50 strike does not make this a $50 purchase.

steps.title: Check the order one last time
steps.explain: Before a practice order, say the ticker, type, expiration, strike, quantity and price aloud. Check the estimated total and fees. A correct calculation cannot rescue an order for the wrong contract.
steps.example: If the ticket shows three contracts instead of two, the cost at $1.80 becomes $540 before fees. Correct the quantity before submitting, not after a fill.

workshop.mistake: A low premium is not automatically good value. It may reflect a small chance of finishing with value or very little time remaining.

challenge.explanation: $1.25 × 100 × 4 = $500. $125 is only one contract; $5 forgets the multiplier.

application.answer: $360 + 2 × $0.65 = $361.30. Selling fees would be a separate cost later. These fees are illustrative, not your broker’s quoted rate.

title: Breakeven and profit
teach: At expiration, a purchased call’s breakeven is strike plus premium; a purchased put’s is strike minus premium, before fees. Before expiration you can sell the option itself. Its sale price determines the result then.
example: Buy one standard call at $2 and sell at $2.40: ($2.40 − $2) × 100 = $40 before fees. A $50 strike call bought at $2 breaks even at a $52 stock price at expiration before fees.
watch: Expiration breakeven is not a requirement for selling an option at a profit earlier.

questions.prompt: Buy at $3 and sell at $2.50. One standard contract loses what before fees?
questions.explanation: Buy one standard call at $2 and sell at $2.40: ($2.40 − $2) × 100 = $40 before fees. A $50 strike call bought at $2 breaks even at a $52 stock price at expiration before fees. Expiration breakeven is not a requirement for selling an option at a profit earlier.

workshop.goal: Separate expiration breakeven from the profit you can make by selling earlier.

steps.title: Name the time you are calculating
steps.explain: Breakeven at expiration asks what stock price would recover the option premium if valued at expiration. It is not the same as the stock price needed to sell the option for a profit today.
steps.example: For a $50 call bought at $2, expiration breakeven is $52 before costs. For a $50 put bought at $2, it is $48.

steps.title: Calculate a sale from the option prices
steps.explain: When you close a purchased option, subtract its entry premium from its sale premium, multiply by 100 and by contracts, then subtract costs. Use the actual sale price for a completed trade.
steps.example: Buy one call at $2 and sell at $2.40: $0.40 × 100 = $40 before fees. This can happen before the stock reaches the expiration breakeven.

steps.title: Include the losing outcomes
steps.explain: A contract can have value and still lose money compared with its purchase cost. At expiration a $50 call with stock at $51 is worth $1 per share intrinsically; paying $2 produces a loss.
steps.example: At stock $51, intrinsic value $100 minus purchase $200 = a $100 loss before costs. At stock $52, the simplified result is zero before costs, not after costs.

workshop.mistake: Breakeven is a calculation, not an order that automatically closes your trade.

challenge.prompt: Buy two standard options at $2.00 and sell both at $2.30 before expiration. What is the result before fees?
challenge.explanation: ($2.30 − $2.00) × 100 × 2 = $60. A completed sale determines the result without waiting for expiration.

application.prompt: A $70 put costs $3. What is its expiration breakeven before fees?
application.answer: $70 − $3 = $67. Below $67 its simplified expiration value exceeds the premium paid; costs lower the net result.

title: Candles tell a finished price story
teach: Each candle has an open, high, low and close. The body connects open and close. Wicks reach the high and low. A completed candle cannot tell you the next candle’s price. Use the Chart workshop to reveal examples one candle at a time.
example: Open $100, high $105, low $99, close $102: price finished $2 above its open, but did not stay at $105.
watch: A candle still forming can change shape and color. Do not describe it as a confirmed close.

questions.prompt: Which value says where a completed candle finished?
questions.explanation: Open $100, high $105, low $99, close $102: price finished $2 above its open, but did not stay at $105. A candle still forming can change shape and color. Do not describe it as a confirmed close.

workshop.goal: Read open, high, low and close, and separate a finished candle from one still changing.

steps.title: Read the body first
steps.explain: A candle summarizes prices over a chosen period. The body runs from the opening price to the closing price. In this lesson green means close above open and red means close below open. Color does not tell you the whole path.
steps.example: Open $50, close $51: the body shows a $1 rise during the period. It does not mean every trade between open and close moved upward.

steps.title: Read the wicks next
steps.explain: The thin lines show the highest and lowest traded prices within that period. Compare the close with those extremes. A close well below the high tells you the price did not stay at its high through the end.
steps.example: Open $50, high $52, low $49, close $51: total range is $3, body is $1, and the close is $1 below the high.

steps.title: Wait for the information you need
steps.explain: A forming candle can change color, high, low and close. If a rule calls for a completed close, its result is not knowable before the period ends. Historical finished candles hide that uncertainty.
steps.example: A 10:00 five-minute candle covers 10:00 up to 10:05 in an open-time labeling system. A breakout at 10:03 can disappear before 10:05. Check how your chart labels bars.

workshop.mistake: One candle does not reveal the exact order in which the high and low happened.

challenge.prompt: A candle opens at $100, reaches $103, falls to $99 and closes at $101. Which is true?
choices: Its range is $4 and body is $1
challenge.explanation: High minus low is $103 − $99 = $4. Close minus open is $101 − $100 = $1. The summary cannot prove a continuous rise.

application.prompt: A candle is green at 10:04, but its five-minute period ends at 10:05. Can you call its final close bullish yet?
application.answer: No. The price can change before 10:05. Record the live observation as provisional and evaluate a close-based rule only when the bar is complete.

title: Timeframes and missing context
teach: A one-minute candle summarizes one minute. A one-hour candle summarizes an hour. They can tell different parts of the same story. A short bounce can happen inside a larger decline.
example: The last three one-minute closes rise from $100 to $101. The hour began at $105. Both a short bounce and an hourly decline can be true.
watch: Check session time and data timestamps. An empty section may be missing data, not a quiet market.

questions.prompt: Can short-term rising candles occur inside a falling hour?
questions.explanation: The last three one-minute closes rise from $100 to $101. The hour began at $105. Both a short bounce and an hourly decline can be true. Check session time and data timestamps. An empty section may be missing data, not a quiet market.

workshop.goal: Compare timeframes without mistaking a short bounce for a larger reversal.

steps.title: Understand what changes when you zoom out
steps.explain: A five-minute candle combines five one-minute periods when all five are available. Its open is the first open, high the highest high, low the lowest low, and close the last close. It is not the average of five closes.
steps.example: One-minute closes of 100, 101, 100.5, 99.5 and 100.2 end the five-minute period at 100.2. They do not show every high or low inside it.

steps.title: Ask two different questions
steps.explain: A small timeframe shows recent movement. A larger timeframe shows a longer sequence. Both can be correct when they disagree. Describe the recent move within the bigger context instead of forcing one label onto both.
steps.example: The last three minutes rise from $98 to $99 while the prior hour fell from $104. That is a short bounce inside the longer decline until more evidence changes the description.

steps.title: Check the window and missing bars
steps.explain: Keep the ticker, timezone, session and last completed timestamp consistent. Missing bars or different session settings can create apparent disagreements. A forming hourly candle is not a finished hour of evidence.
steps.example: At 10:17, a chart whose hourly bars start at 9:30 has not completed its 9:30 bar. Use the last completed hour if your rule needs completed candles.

workshop.mistake: Changing chart timeframe changes the view, not the historical facts or your trade’s existing rules.

challenge.prompt: The last three one-minute closes rise, but the completed hourly trend falls. What can you conclude?
choices: A short bounce can exist within a longer decline
challenge.explanation: The two charts summarize different lengths of time. The bounce alone does not establish that the larger decline has ended.

application.prompt: Five-minute closes are present at 10:00 and 10:10 but 10:05 is absent. Should you treat the gap as a flat candle?
application.answer: No. Mark missing data. A flat candle would invent an open, high, low and close that were never observed.

title: Higher highs and higher lows
teach: A higher high exceeds an earlier swing high. A higher low stays above an earlier swing low. Lower highs and lower lows mirror this. A swing is a turning area; a rule may need later candles to confirm it.
example: Lows of $100 then $102 and highs of $104 then $106 describe rising structure. The turning point may not have been knowable at the exact lowest price.
watch: Do not use a later-confirmed arrow as if it was visible earlier.

questions.prompt: A low at $102 after a low at $100 is what?
questions.explanation: Lows of $100 then $102 and highs of $104 then $106 describe rising structure. The turning point may not have been knowable at the exact lowest price. Do not use a later-confirmed arrow as if it was visible earlier.

workshop.goal: Identify an upward structure from confirmed swing points rather than one green candle.

steps.title: Find turning points
steps.explain: A swing high is a local peak and a swing low is a local valley under a chosen rule. You need later observations to confirm a turn. The moment a price makes a high is not automatically the moment it becomes a confirmed swing.
steps.example: For this exercise, a high must have a lower high on each side. The right-side candle must finish before you can label the middle candle.

steps.title: Compare like with like
steps.explain: Compare the new confirmed high with the preceding high, and the new confirmed low with the preceding low. Higher highs and higher lows describe an upward sequence. Comparing a low to a high tells you something different.
steps.example: Highs $101 then $103 and lows $99 then $100 form a rising structure. A single close at $102 does not supply all four swing points.

steps.title: Keep the conclusion proportional
steps.explain: Structure describes what has happened; it does not guarantee continuation. If a higher low breaks, investigate whether the upward description still fits. Do not move the old low to protect your prediction.
steps.example: A later completed close below the recorded $100 higher low is adverse evidence. Whether it triggers an exit depends on the written policy, not the chart label alone.

workshop.mistake: Do not backdate a swing label to claim a signal was available before its confirming candle.

challenge.prompt: Confirmed highs are $105 then $107; lows are $102 then $103. Which description fits?
challenge.explanation: Compare highs with highs: 107 exceeds 105. Compare lows with lows: 103 exceeds 102. Both parts of the structure rise.

application.prompt: A peak at 10:05 requires the 10:06 candle to confirm it. When may a rule using that peak first act?
application.answer: After the 10:06 candle is complete and received. The marker can point at 10:05, but the information became knowable later.

title: Support, resistance and breaks
teach: Support is an area where buying previously helped stop a decline. Resistance is where selling previously slowed a rise. Neither is a wall. A break means price moved through a level; whether a strategy needs a touch or a close is a separate rule.
example: Price reaches above $102 but closes at $101. A rule needing a close above $102 has not passed. A rule based on an intrabar touch is different.
watch: A line drawn on a chart is not automatically an active stop order.

questions.prompt: Does every chart support line automatically sell your option?
questions.explanation: Price reaches above $102 but closes at $101. A rule needing a close above $102 has not passed. A rule based on an intrabar touch is different. A line drawn on a chart is not automatically an active stop order.

workshop.goal: Draw a price reference from prior reactions and distinguish a touch from a confirmed break.

steps.title: Treat levels as areas of interest
steps.explain: Support is an area where falling price previously found buying. Resistance is where rising price previously stalled. Several reactions can make a level worth watching, but do not make it an invisible wall.
steps.example: If price repeatedly turns near $50.00 to $50.15, record a zone rather than pretending every reversal happens at exactly $50.00.

steps.title: Write what counts as a break
steps.explain: A brief trade through a level, a completed close beyond it and multiple closes beyond it are different rules. Choose one before looking at the outcome. A more demanding confirmation usually arrives later.
steps.example: Practice rule: a completed close below $50 counts as a support break. A low of $49.80 followed by a $50.20 close does not meet that specific rule.

steps.title: Keep references separate from orders
steps.explain: A support line is information. It only becomes a protective stop when the execution policy monitors and acts on it. Even a triggered stop does not guarantee the intended sale price.
steps.example: A chart can show $50 support while the active policy exits on an option-premium condition. Read the actual policy before assuming the line limits your loss.

workshop.mistake: A broken support area can later act as resistance, but that reaction must be observed rather than assumed.

challenge.explanation: The rule uses the close, not the low or color. $80.10 is above $80, so this candle does not satisfy it.

application.prompt: Write two different rules for breaking $50 support and explain their timing.
application.answer: A real-time trade below $50 can trigger during a candle. A completed close below $50 waits for the candle to finish. Neither is automatically better; they create different decisions.

title: Averages and VWAP
teach: A simple moving average averages recent prices. A 9 SMA uses nine bars; a 200 SMA uses 200. VWAP weights prices by traded volume during its defined session. These describe price context, not guaranteed future moves.
example: On a five-minute chart, nine bars cover 45 minutes of bar intervals. The same nine-bar average on a one-minute chart covers nine minutes.
watch: The number of bars and the timeframe both matter.

questions.prompt: Does a 9 SMA describe the same time span on 1m and 5m charts?
questions.explanation: On a five-minute chart, nine bars cover 45 minutes of bar intervals. The same nine-bar average on a one-minute chart covers nine minutes. The number of bars and the timeframe both matter.

workshop.goal: Explain what a moving average and VWAP summarize, without treating either as a prediction.

steps.title: Average a fixed number of observations
steps.explain: A simple moving average adds the last N closes and divides by N. As each new completed close arrives, the oldest one drops out. An exponential average puts more weight on recent observations. They are different calculations.
steps.example: Closes $10, $12 and $11 give a three-close SMA of $11. Add a $13 close and drop $10: the new SMA is $12.

steps.title: Understand volume weighting
steps.explain: VWAP gives larger-volume trades more influence on an average price. A session VWAP commonly restarts each session; an anchored VWAP starts from a chosen event. Identify the anchor and price/volume source before comparing lines.
steps.example: In a simplified two-trade example, 100 shares at $10 and 300 at $12 give ($1,000 + $3,600) ÷ 400 = $11.50 VWAP, not $11.

steps.title: Use location and slope carefully
steps.explain: Price above an average says where price is relative to its history. Slope describes how the average changes. Neither condition guarantees the next candle. Warmup, timeframe and session boundaries affect the result.
steps.example: A 200-period average on one-minute candles is not the same as a 200-period average on hourly candles. They summarize very different lengths of history.

workshop.mistake: A VWAP touch is not an automatic entry. The strategy may also require direction, candle shape, volume and execution checks.

challenge.prompt: 100 shares trade at $20 and 300 shares at $22. What is the simplified VWAP?
challenge.explanation: Total value is $2,000 + $6,600 = $8,600. Divide by 400 shares to get $21.50. The larger trade gets more weight.

application.prompt: A three-close SMA uses 20, 21, 22. The next close is 26. What is the new SMA?
application.answer: Drop 20. (21 + 22 + 26) ÷ 3 = 23. The old average was 21. The line responds after new price information arrives.

title: RSI, MACD and volume
teach: RSI summarizes recent gains relative to losses on a scale from 0 to 100. MACD compares moving averages; its signal line smooths MACD, and its histogram shows their difference. Volume counts shares traded. None can promise a reversal.
example: RSI below 30 is often called oversold. Price can still keep falling. A MACD cross describes a change in its averages, not an order instruction by itself.
watch: An indicator only becomes an execution trigger if the active strategy explicitly uses it.

questions.prompt: Does low RSI guarantee a rebound?
questions.explanation: RSI below 30 is often called oversold. Price can still keep falling. A MACD cross describes a change in its averages, not an order instruction by itself. An indicator only becomes an execution trigger if the active strategy explicitly uses it.

workshop.goal: Read momentum and participation as context, and state what an indicator cannot tell you.

steps.title: Read RSI as a recent-movement summary
steps.explain: RSI compares recent upward and downward price changes on a scale from 0 to 100. Its value depends on the lookback and calculation method. A high reading can persist during a strong rise rather than forcing an immediate fall.
steps.example: An RSI above 70 is often called overbought. That is a description of the indicator, not proof that selling now will make money.

steps.title: Separate MACD’s three parts
steps.explain: MACD commonly subtracts a slower exponential average from a faster one. Its signal is a smoothed MACD line. The histogram is MACD minus signal. A cross describes a change between those lines, not a guaranteed change in profit.
steps.example: MACD 0.30 minus signal 0.20 gives histogram +0.10. If MACD becomes 0.15 while signal stays 0.20, the histogram is −0.05.

steps.title: Ask whether activity supports the story
steps.explain: Volume measures how much traded over a period. Compare similar session times and durations. Indicators and price must use matching candles; mixing an hourly RSI with a one-minute chart can mislead you.
steps.example: A quiet lunch candle should not be judged against the opening minute without context. High volume alone also does not reveal whether the next move will rise or fall.

workshop.mistake: RSI, MACD and volume can disagree. Describe the disagreement instead of inventing certainty or a universal buy signal.

challenge.prompt: MACD is 0.12 and signal is 0.18. What is the histogram?
challenge.explanation: Subtract signal from MACD: 0.12 −0.18 = −0.06. This is a relationship between lines, not a forecast of an option’s return.

application.prompt: RSI is 75 while price keeps making higher lows. Must the next candle fall?
application.answer: No. RSI can stay elevated. Inspect the actual price sequence and your written rule; the reading alone cannot establish an immediate reversal.

title: Bid, ask and spread
teach: The bid is a displayed buying price. The ask is a displayed selling price. The spread is the gap between them. For a purchased option, a bid can help estimate a sale, but its size and age matter.
example: An option bid is $2.00 and ask $2.20. Buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses $20 per standard contract before fees, even without a market move.
watch: A quote is not a fill. A small displayed size may not cover all your contracts.

questions.prompt: What is the before-fee spread cost in the example?
questions.explanation: An option bid is $2.00 and ask $2.20. Buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses $20 per standard contract before fees, even without a market move. A quote is not a fill. A small displayed size may not cover all your contracts.

workshop.goal: Estimate the cost of crossing the spread and recognize a quote that needs checking.

steps.title: Know which side you can trade against
steps.explain: The bid is an advertised buying price; the ask is an advertised selling price. A buyer seeking immediate execution often pays near the ask, while a seller often receives near the bid. Quotes can change before an order reaches them.
steps.example: Bid $2.00, ask $2.20: buying at $2.20 and immediately selling at $2.00 loses $20 per standard contract before fees.

steps.title: Do not spend the midpoint on paper
steps.explain: The midpoint is halfway between bid and ask. It is a useful reference, not a promised fill. A limit at the midpoint may wait, partially fill or never fill.
steps.example: The midpoint of $2.00/$2.20 is $2.10. Marking a purchased option at $2.10 does not prove somebody would buy your entire position there.

steps.title: Check timestamp and size
steps.explain: A fresh quote with enough displayed size is more informative than an old last trade. A crossed quote, where bid exceeds ask, needs validation. Never quietly replace a missing bid with a convenient price to claim a profit.
steps.example: A $2.50 last trade from 20 minutes ago cannot establish your sale proceeds now. Find a current bid for the exact contract and check available size.

workshop.mistake: The spread is already reflected when you model entry at ask and exit at bid. Do not subtract the same spread again.

challenge.prompt: Buy at $1.60 ask and sell at $1.50 bid with no price change. What is one contract’s result before fees?
challenge.explanation: ($1.50 − $1.60) × 100 = − $10. The quoted spread created the loss even though the market did not move.

application.prompt: The bid is missing but midpoint is $2.10. Can you report a sell at $2.10?
application.answer: No. Mark the sale unpriced or wait for usable data. A midpoint is not a confirmed executable bid or a fill.

title: Market orders, limits and fills
teach: A market order prioritizes execution but does not guarantee price. A limit order sets a price boundary but may not fill. A partial fill means only some contracts traded. Track the remaining quantity before sending another order.
example: You try to sell four contracts with a $2 minimum. Two fill at $2.05; two remain open. You have sold two, not four.
watch: Sending a duplicate sell can create unintended exposure. Check order status first.

questions.prompt: Two of four contracts filled. How many remain?
questions.explanation: You try to sell four contracts with a $2 minimum. Two fill at $2.05; two remain open. You have sold two, not four. Sending a duplicate sell can create unintended exposure. Check order status first.

workshop.goal: Choose between price control and execution urgency, then verify what actually filled.

steps.title: A market order prioritizes execution
steps.explain: A market order requests execution at available prices. It does not lock the price displayed when you click. Fast movement, wide spreads and small size can make the average fill worse than expected.
steps.example: You see an ask of $2.00, but it disappears before arrival. A market buy may fill at $2.10 or another available price.

steps.title: A limit order controls acceptable price
steps.explain: A buy limit sets the highest price you accept. A sell limit sets the lowest. It may fill at the limit or better, but it may not fill at all. A stop and a stop-limit introduce different trigger and execution behavior.
steps.example: A buy limit of $2.00 cannot intentionally pay $2.10. If no seller offers $2.00 or less, the order remains unfilled under its time-in-force rules.

steps.title: Reconcile the result
steps.explain: Submitted, accepted, partially filled and filled are separate states. Before sending another order, check the existing order and position. Otherwise a retry can accidentally double the quantity.
steps.example: You request 5 contracts and 2 fill. You own 2, while 3 may still be working. A second request for 5 could eventually leave you with 10, not 5.

workshop.mistake: A cancellation request is not proof that an order was canceled before a fill occurred.

challenge.prompt: A buy limit is $2.00 and the lowest ask is $2.10. What can happen?
challenge.explanation: The limit prevents paying above $2.00. Execution is not guaranteed while sellers ask more.

application.prompt: You requested 6 contracts and the broker confirms 4 filled. What should your position count show?
application.answer: 4 filled contracts, plus a separate record of the remaining 2 working or canceled. Do not count all 6 as owned until confirmed.

title: Why direction can be right and the option lose
teach: Option value depends on more than stock direction. Time remaining and expected future movement also matter. Intrinsic value is the value of exercising now; time value is premium above intrinsic value.
example: A call bought before news can lose value afterward even if the stock rises slightly, because expectations of future movement fall.
watch: A correct stock prediction is not enough to prove a profitable option trade.

questions.prompt: Can a call lose value while its stock rises?
questions.explanation: A call bought before news can lose value afterward even if the stock rises slightly, because expectations of future movement fall. A correct stock prediction is not enough to prove a profitable option trade.

workshop.goal: Explain why getting stock direction right may still produce an option loss.

steps.title: The option has more than one influence
steps.explain: An option’s price responds to the underlying, remaining time, expected future movement and other inputs. A call can lose value while its stock rises if other influences outweigh that move.
steps.example: Stock rises 1%, but a call bought for $3 can still bid $2.70 later. The stock chart alone does not determine the option’s current sale price.

steps.title: Time and expectations matter
steps.explain: The value beyond immediate exercise value can shrink as expiration approaches or expected volatility falls. Implied volatility is the market’s pricing of uncertainty, not a promise of how far price will move.
steps.example: Before an announcement, buyers may pay for a large possible move. After a small move, uncertainty can fall and the option premium can shrink.

steps.title: Diagnose using the contract’s own record
steps.explain: Compare entry and exit option quotes, timestamp, spread, days remaining and volatility context. Do not call every loss a bad chart signal without checking whether the contract was expensive or hard to sell.
steps.example: If the entry was $3.00 ask and later bid $2.70, the result is − $30 per contract before costs. A rising stock does not reverse that arithmetic.

workshop.mistake: Use “may have contributed” when the record cannot isolate time, volatility and price effects. Do not invent exact causes from a chart alone.

choices: It made money because the stock rose
The recorded option loss is impossible
It lost $20 per standard contract before fees

application.prompt: What three records would help explain that loss?
application.answer: The exact contract’s timestamped entry/exit quotes and fills; time remaining to expiration; and available volatility/spread context. Missing inputs should remain missing.

title: Meet the Greeks
teach: Delta estimates option-price sensitivity to a small stock move. Gamma describes how delta changes. Theta estimates time-decay sensitivity. Vega estimates sensitivity to implied volatility. These are estimates that change with conditions.
example: A delta of 0.50 suggests roughly a $0.50 option move for a $1 stock move, with other factors held constant. It is not a promise.
watch: Delta is not a guaranteed profit or a guaranteed chance of winning.

questions.prompt: Which Greek describes sensitivity to time passing?
questions.explanation: A delta of 0.50 suggests roughly a $0.50 option move for a $1 stock move, with other factors held constant. It is not a promise. Delta is not a guaranteed profit or a guaranteed chance of winning.

workshop.goal: Use the Greeks as estimates of different risks, not as guarantees.

steps.title: Delta and gamma concern stock movement
steps.explain: Delta estimates how much option premium changes for a small $1 underlying move, holding other inputs fixed. Gamma estimates how delta itself changes. A call’s delta is usually positive and a purchased put’s usually negative.
steps.example: A call delta 0.40 suggests about $0.40 premium change for a small $1 stock rise, or $40 per standard contract. That estimate can change as price moves.

steps.title: Theta and vega concern time and uncertainty
steps.explain: Theta estimates the effect of time passing; vega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility. Units matter. These estimates hold other inputs constant, which a real market rarely does.
steps.example: Theta −0.05 suggests roughly $5 per contract for a day under the model. Vega 0.10 suggests about $10 per contract for a one-point volatility change.

steps.title: Combine the story without pretending precision
steps.explain: A favorable delta effect can be offset by time, volatility and trading costs. Large moves need a fresh estimate. Do not add rough one-factor calculations and label the result a guaranteed executable quote.
steps.example: A model suggests +$20 from price and − $15 from volatility: the rough net is +$5 before other effects and costs. The actual bid remains the sale reference.

workshop.mistake: Delta is not a literal percent chance of making a profitable trade. Profit also depends on the amount paid and when you exit.

challenge.prompt: A call has delta 0.30. For a small $1 stock rise, all else fixed, what is its rough premium change per standard contract?
challenge.explanation: 0.30 × $1 × 100 = about $30. It is a sensitivity estimate, not a promised fill or profit.

application.prompt: Which estimate addresses the passage of time rather than a stock move?
application.answer: Theta. A negative daily theta describes modeled premium erosion with other inputs fixed; actual changes also include market movement and other factors.

title: Size from a defined risk plan
teach: First define how the trade will be exited. Then estimate loss per contract, including costs and execution uncertainty. A stop is not a guaranteed sale price. If reliable stop risk cannot be established, do not pretend it is known.
example: In a paper example, entry $2 and planned exit $1.50 imply $50 per standard contract before costs. A $100 risk allowance fits two only before adding costs and uncertainty. It does not guarantee a $100 maximum loss.
watch: Buying more contracts because the premium looks cheap can increase risk sharply.

questions.prompt: Do fees and slippage need room in a risk estimate?
questions.explanation: In a paper example, entry $2 and planned exit $1.50 imply $50 per standard contract before costs. A $100 risk allowance fits two only before adding costs and uncertainty. It does not guarantee a $100 maximum loss. Buying more contracts because the premium looks cheap can increase risk sharply.

workshop.goal: Distinguish a planned loss from money actually exposed, and round quantities down.

steps.title: Start with a dollar budget
steps.explain: Convert an account percentage into dollars before considering quantity. A budget is a limit you choose, not a forecast of the loss. Different positions can consume the same account budget at the same time.
steps.example: A $10,000 practice account with a 2% budget has $200 available under that rule. This example is not a recommended percentage or a change to your settings.

steps.title: Choose a defensible per-contract assumption
steps.explain: A stop-based loss estimate only makes sense when the stop is actually monitored and executable, and even then gaps can make losses worse. For a purchased option, the full premium plus costs is a more conservative exposure assumption.
steps.example: At $2 per share and an illustrative $1.30 round-trip fee, full-cost exposure is $201.30 per contract. A $200 budget cannot cover one contract under that assumption.

steps.title: Apply every limit
steps.explain: Divide the budget by the assumed per-contract exposure and round down. Then apply purchase-cost, buying-power, contract and account limits. The smallest valid quantity wins. Zero is a valid answer.
steps.example: A $500 budget divided by $201.30 permits 2 contracts, not 3. A separate purchase cap permitting only 1 makes the final ceiling 1.

workshop.mistake: Do not size from a support line that the execution engine does not enforce. A reference line cannot promise a small loss.

application.prompt: Risk budget allows 3 contracts but purchase cap allows 2. Which quantity is the ceiling?
application.answer: 2. Both limits must hold. Other checks may reduce that further or block the trade.

title: Profit targets, trails and safety exits
teach: A target exits at a specified gain. A trailing exit follows a peak and gives back part of that gain. A time exit and a safety exit serve different purposes. Read the actual policy; teaching examples do not change CELO settings.
example: Buy at $2, peak at $2.40: peak profit is $40 per contract. A 25% giveback of profit is $10, so the reference exit is $2.30 before costs, not $1.80.
watch: A gap or stale quote can prevent execution at the reference level.

questions.prompt: 25% of a $40 peak profit is how much?
questions.explanation: Buy at $2, peak at $2.40: peak profit is $40 per contract. A 25% giveback of profit is $10, so the reference exit is $2.30 before costs, not $1.80. A gap or stale quote can prevent execution at the reference level.

workshop.goal: Explain targets, trailing profit rules and safety exits without mixing their purposes.

steps.title: A target reacts to reaching a level
steps.explain: A fixed premium-gain target compares current option price with entry. It can sell all or part of a position. State the price basis and fraction sold; “take profit at 10%” is incomplete without them.
steps.example: An option bought at $2 reaches a 10% gain at $2.20. Selling 3 of 6 contracts there locks in $60 before fees on those 3 only.

steps.title: A giveback follows the profit peak
steps.explain: A peak-profit giveback compares current profit with the highest observed profit after the rule arms. Giving back 10% of profit is not the same as falling 10% from the option’s peak price.
steps.example: Entry $2, peak bid $2.50: peak profit $50 per contract. A 10% profit giveback is $5, placing the theoretical threshold at $2.45, not $2.25.

steps.title: Safety exits solve different problems
steps.explain: A loss stop, a time limit, a session-close rule and an emergency response have different triggers. Read which are actually active. A profit rule that never arms cannot protect a trade before it becomes profitable.
steps.example: If a target requires +10% and the option only declines, that target never activates. The existing loss and safety rules must determine what happens next.

workshop.mistake: A threshold is a signal, not a guaranteed sale price. Quotes, available size and order fills determine actual proceeds.

challenge.prompt: Entry $3, peak bid $3.60, giveback 25% of peak profit. What is the theoretical threshold?
challenge.explanation: Peak profit is $60 per contract. 25% is $15. Retained profit $45 means $3.45 option price. This ignores execution costs and gaps.

application.prompt: If six contracts are held and half sell, how many still need management?
application.answer: Three. Record the first sale and keep monitoring the remaining three. A partial sale does not mean the whole position is closed.

steps.text: That leaves $4.75. It is a theoretical threshold before fees, gaps and fill uncertainty, not a guaranteed sale price.

title: Separate setup, trigger and permission
teach: A setup is a pattern worth watching. A trigger is the specific condition for acting. Permission includes available buying power, acceptable quotes and safety checks. A pattern alone does not mean an order should be placed.
example: For an illustrative pullback: watch a return to a level, wait for the written recovery condition, check the contract and risk, then record a pretend entry. If a check fails, record why you skipped.
watch: Do not mix different entry and exit rules just because their separate results looked good.

questions.prompt: Does a good-looking setup mean all order checks passed?
questions.explanation: For an illustrative pullback: watch a return to a level, wait for the written recovery condition, check the contract and risk, then record a pretend entry. If a check fails, record why you skipped. Do not mix different entry and exit rules just because their separate results looked good.

workshop.goal: Separate a chart opportunity from an approved executable order.

steps.title: A setup describes a situation
steps.explain: A setup is a pattern or context worth watching. It does not mean every entry condition passed. Give it a precise name and record the observations that created interest.
steps.example: Price is near VWAP after a pullback. That may be a setup, while the strategy still waits for a completed rejection candle.

steps.title: A trigger completes the chart condition
steps.explain: The trigger is the specific event the chart rule requires. Record its time and the candle used. A trigger is still separate from checks on the option contract and the account.
steps.example: The rejection candle closes at 10:35. The chart trigger becomes available then, not halfway through the candle.

steps.title: Permission and execution come afterward
steps.explain: The account may reject an otherwise valid chart trigger for stale prices, wide spread, insufficient buying power, position limits or a safety halt. Only broker fills establish ownership.
steps.example: A chart passes but the exact option has no valid bid/ask. The bot should explain that pricing blocked entry rather than pretend the strategy never saw a setup.

workshop.mistake: “Chart passed” does not mean “order filled.” Keep each stage visible and traceable.

challenge.prompt: A setup triggered, but the broker has not filled the submitted order. How many contracts are confirmed owned?
challenge.explanation: An order request is not a position. Use confirmed fills, including partial fills, to establish ownership.

application.prompt: Write a useful reason for a skipped setup with a stale quote.
application.answer: “The chart trigger passed at 10:35, but the option quote was 4 minutes old. Entry was skipped because the pricing check required a fresher quote.” Example limit only.

title: Review a whole trade honestly
teach: Record the setup, contract, quantity, entry, planned exits, actual exits and costs. Compare what you planned with what happened. Keep losses and missing data visible. Several wins are not proof of a dependable method.
example: Buy two standard contracts at $2 and sell at $2.20: gross profit $40. With $6 total costs, net profit is $34. Review whether the entry and exit followed the plan, not just the green number.
watch: Practice completion shows knowledge, not readiness for real-money trading or guaranteed returns.

questions.prompt: What is the example’s net profit?
questions.explanation: Buy two standard contracts at $2 and sell at $2.20: gross profit $40. With $6 total costs, net profit is $34. Review whether the entry and exit followed the plan, not just the green number. Practice completion shows knowledge, not readiness for real-money trading or guaranteed returns.

workshop.goal: Reconstruct a trade from records and separate a good decision from a good outcome.

steps.title: Start at entry, not the best-looking later candle
steps.explain: Save the information available when the decision was made: candle time, contract, entry quote, quantity and rules. A later chart can make an earlier decision look more obvious than it was.
steps.example: If a swing was confirmed at 10:12, it cannot justify an entry at 10:10. Keep the event time and the time information became available.

steps.title: Explain each change in the position
steps.explain: Record partial sales, remaining quantity, quote timestamps and reasons. Separate a hypothetical better exit from what the broker actually filled. Use fees consistently when calculating results.
steps.example: Buy 4 at $2.00; sell 2 at $2.20 and 2 at $1.80. The first sale gains $40 and the second loses $40, so total is zero before fees.

steps.title: Choose one improvement to test
steps.explain: Classify the problem: entry, contract selection, sizing, exit, execution or missing evidence. A single loss cannot prove which rule is best. Test an explicit change on comparable trades and keep incomplete ones labeled.
steps.example: If an exit was late because the worker stopped, fix execution first. Changing a strategy threshold does not diagnose the stalled worker.

workshop.mistake: The best price visible afterward is hindsight. Do not describe it as an exit the bot could necessarily have taken.

application.prompt: A quote is missing at a proposed exit time. Can you claim that alternate exit won?
application.answer: No. Mark the result incomplete. Recover properly timestamped data if available, preserving its source; do not substitute the later peak.

title: Read the whole option name
teach: A ticker alone does not identify an option. Read the stock, expiration date, call or put, and strike together. Two contracts on the same stock can behave very differently. A call gives its buyer a right to buy shares at the strike; a put gives a right to sell. Buying either is different from selling an option to open a short position.
example: ABC November 20 $100 call and ABC November 27 $100 call have the same strike but different time remaining. A displayed $2 premium normally means $200 for one standard 100-share contract, before costs. Check the contract multiplier because adjusted contracts can differ.
watch: Before any paper order, read its identity aloud. A right direction on the wrong contract is still the wrong trade.

questions.prompt: What identifies a specific option?
choices: Ticker, expiration, call or put, and strike
questions.explanation: The complete identity prevents a different expiration, strike or option type from being mistaken for your intended contract.

workshop.goal: Decode a contract name and catch a wrong-contract mistake before an order.

steps.title: Read from identity to terms
steps.explain: Start with ticker, then expiration, then call or put, then strike. Each field changes what you own. A familiar company name does not make every contract interchangeable.
steps.example: XYZ June 18 $50 call is different from XYZ June 18 $55 call. The latter requires a higher stock price for intrinsic value at expiration.

steps.title: Separate the contract name from its quote
steps.explain: The name identifies the instrument. Bid and ask describe current prices for that instrument. The strike stays fixed under normal terms while the quote changes during trading.
steps.example: A $50 call can have a $2.10 ask at one moment and $2.30 later. Neither quote changes its $50 strike.

steps.title: Verify the multiplier and action
steps.explain: Check standard versus adjusted terms, quantity, and whether the action opens or closes a position. Do not infer a ticker from a shortened label if the full contract is available.
steps.example: Buying to open one put and selling to close that same put are two actions on one instrument. Selling to open would create a different position.

workshop.mistake: Always match the exact contract in entry records, quotes and exit orders. Same ticker is not enough.

challenge.prompt: Which pair describes the same contract?
choices: Same ticker and strike, different expiration
Same ticker, expiration, type and strike with matching terms
challenge.explanation: Identity depends on the full contract terms, not its premium. Expiration and type are essential even when the ticker and strike match.

application.prompt: Your plan says July $60 put, but the ticket says July $60 call. What needs correction?
application.answer: The option type. Stop and select the put before ordering. A call does not become equivalent because its premium is similar.

title: Expiration is part of the plan
teach: Expiration is the date the contract ends. More time can cost more, but it does not guarantee a profit. Less time leaves less opportunity for the expected move to happen. Start with how long your idea needs, then examine available contracts. Do not choose the cheapest contract just because its price looks small.
example: Your idea may take three days, but a contract expires this afternoon. That contract cannot wait for your three-day plan. A longer-dated contract can still lose if the stock moves against you or the market prices in less uncertainty.
watch: Write the planned holding period and expiration on separate lines. They are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: Which contract can outlast a three-day idea?
choices: One with time beyond the planned holding period
Every contract lasts until you sell
questions.explanation: A contract must still exist when your planned move might happen. Enough time is necessary, not a promise of a good trade.

workshop.goal: Choose an expiration by the time the idea needs, while recognizing its tradeoffs.

steps.title: Count the time available
steps.explain: Expiration is the contract’s deadline, not the planned exit time. A trade intended to last 30 minutes can use a contract expiring later. The plan still needs an exit if the move does not happen.
steps.example: A Friday-expiring contract held on Thursday gives less time than one expiring next month, even if both have the same strike.

steps.title: Compare price and sensitivity
steps.explain: Longer-dated options often cost more because they contain more time value. Short-dated options may look cheaper but can change quickly and lose remaining time value rapidly. Cheap is not the same as forgiving.
steps.example: A $1 near-expiry option and a $4 later-expiry option expose different dollars and sensitivities. Do not compare them as if only price changed.

steps.title: Plan around the deadline
steps.explain: Know broker cutoff and settlement procedures before approaching expiration. Corporate events and market closures can affect the practical timeline. Do not assume a chart remaining open means an option can still be traded.
steps.example: A plan to “check tomorrow” is unsuitable if the contract expires today. Review the contract and broker instructions before the deadline, not afterward.

workshop.mistake: Days to expiration alone cannot tell you which contract will earn more. Compare the actual quotes, liquidity and intended holding period.

challenge.prompt: A trade plan needs several days to develop, but the option expires today. What is the main mismatch?
choices: The contract deadline may arrive before the idea can develop
challenge.explanation: The contract may end before the planned move has time to happen. The expiration must fit the plan; it does not extend itself.

application.prompt: Does buying a later expiration require holding until that date?
application.answer: No. A purchased option can be sold to close earlier when trading is available. Expiration and planned holding time are separate.

title: In, at and out of the money
teach: These terms compare the stock price with the strike. A call is in the money when the stock is above its strike; a put is in the money when the stock is below its strike. At the money means close to the strike. Out of the money means exercising has no immediate value. None of these labels says whether your purchase has made money.
example: ABC is $103. Its $100 call has $3 of immediate exercise value. If you paid $5 for it, that $3 does not mean a $3 profit. You must compare what you paid with what you could receive when selling.
watch: In the money describes a contract, not your personal profit.

questions.prompt: A stock is $103 and its call strike is $100. What do you know?
choices: The call is in the money
questions.explanation: The call has immediate exercise value, but profit depends on the price paid, sale price and costs.

workshop.goal: Determine whether a call or put has intrinsic value without confusing that with profit.

steps.title: Compare stock with strike
steps.explain: A call is in the money when stock is above strike. A put is in the money when stock is below strike. At the money usually means stock is near strike. Out of the money means no immediate intrinsic value.
steps.example: At stock $52, a $50 call is in the money and a $50 put is out of the money. The direction of the comparison reverses for puts.

steps.title: Calculate intrinsic value
steps.explain: For a call, use max(stock −strike,0). For a put, use max(strike −stock,0). Multiply by 100 for a standard contract. Before expiration, the premium can exceed intrinsic value.
steps.example: At stock $52, the $50 call has $2 per share of intrinsic value. If quoted at $3, the extra $1 is value beyond immediate exercise value.

steps.title: Calculate profit separately
steps.explain: In the money describes a relationship between stock and strike. Profit compares what you receive with what you paid, including costs. An in-the-money option can still be a losing purchase.
steps.example: Pay $4 for the call and value it at $2 at expiration: the simplified loss is $200 per contract before fees despite being in the money.

workshop.mistake: Out of the money before expiration does not mean an option has a zero market price.

challenge.prompt: Stock $45, put strike $50. What is intrinsic value per share?
challenge.explanation: A right to sell at $50 when stock is $45 has $5 per share of intrinsic value. Profit still depends on premium paid.

application.prompt: A $50 call is worth $3 at expiration after you paid $4. Is it profitable?
application.answer: No. Its $300 value is $100 below the $400 purchase cost per standard contract before fees.

title: Breakeven is not a stop
teach: At expiration, a standard long call breaks even before fees at strike plus premium paid. A long put breaks even at strike minus premium. Before expiration, time and uncertainty also affect the option price. You can sell for a profit before the stock reaches the expiration breakeven, or lose even while the contract is in the money.
example: Pay $2 for a $100 call. Its expiration breakeven is $102 before fees. If its bid rises to $2.30 before expiration, selling one standard contract would show $30 gross gain, even if the stock has not reached $102.
watch: Breakeven is a calculation for a stated time. A stop is a planned action if the trade goes wrong.

questions.prompt: A $100 call costs $2. Its expiration breakeven before fees is:
questions.explanation: The stock must be $2 above the strike at expiration to cover the $2 premium, before fees.

workshop.goal: Keep an expiration calculation separate from an active exit instruction.

steps.title: Calculate breakeven in its proper setting
steps.explain: Expiration breakeven for a purchased call is strike plus premium; for a purchased put it is strike minus premium, before costs. It assumes expiration valuation rather than a sale at an earlier market quote.
steps.example: A $100 call bought for $4 has a $104 expiration breakeven before fees. That number does not tell the platform when to exit.

steps.title: Define the actual stop
steps.explain: A stop specifies an observable trigger and the action to take. It might use stock price, option bid or another rule. It must be configured and enforced to do anything.
steps.example: “Sell if option bid falls to $3” is a rule about the option. “Expiration breakeven $104” is a stock-price calculation. They are not substitutes.

steps.title: Separate signal from proceeds
steps.explain: When a stop triggers, the final sale can differ because of spread, gaps, size or delay. A stop-limit adds a price restriction but may remain unfilled. Monitor the position until fills confirm it is closed.
steps.example: A $3 trigger does not guarantee a $3 sale. If the next available bid is $2.70, a market exit can realize a larger loss.

workshop.mistake: Do not wait for a breakeven stock price merely because it appears on the contract screen. Follow the approved exit plan.

challenge.prompt: A contract screen displays breakeven $104. No exit order or monitored rule exists. What happens automatically at $104?
choices: Nothing is implied by that number alone
challenge.explanation: Breakeven is information, not an order. An explicit execution rule is needed to act.

application.prompt: Call strike $80, entry premium $3, option stop bid $2.40. Name the two different numbers.
application.answer: Expiration breakeven is stock $83 before costs. The stop watches option bid $2.40. A sale at that bid would lose $60 per standard contract before fees.

title: Higher highs and higher lows
teach: A higher high means a swing peak is above an earlier swing peak. A higher low means a pullback bottom is above an earlier bottom. Together they describe a rising structure, not a guarantee of the next candle. The label needs a consistent confirmation rule. If you wait for a later candle to identify a swing, you could not have known that label at the earlier peak.
example: Price rises from $100 to $103, pulls back to $101, then rises above $103. The new high and higher pullback can support a bullish interpretation. If your swing rule requires two later candles, the $101 low becomes confirmed only after those candles finish.
watch: Keep both the swing time and the time it became knowable. Do not trade a hindsight arrow.

questions.prompt: When could a two-later-candle swing rule know the low?
choices: At the low before it happens
After the two required candles close
questions.explanation: The confirming candles must exist before the rule can act.

workshop.goal: Track the sequence of highs and lows and recognize what would weaken it.

steps.title: Make swing confirmation explicit
steps.explain: Use one fixed swing rule when comparing examples. For this exercise a turning point needs a completed candle on both sides with lower highs for a peak or higher lows for a valley. Flat ties are not confirmed by this strict rule.
steps.example: A high at bar 3 is confirmed only after bar 4 closes with a lower high. Label the point at bar 3, but record bar 4 as the confirmation time.

steps.title: Build the sequence
steps.explain: List confirmed highs and lows separately. An upward structure requires progress in both lists. A higher high with a lower low can indicate expansion or conflict rather than a clean rising sequence.
steps.example: Highs 101→104 and lows 99→102 rise together. Highs 101→104 but lows 99→98 do not describe the same orderly structure.

steps.title: Identify the level that matters next
steps.explain: The latest confirmed higher low is a reference for the current structure. A breach may weaken the bullish description, but the execution rule must specify how to act. Do not retrospectively select whichever low looks best.
steps.example: In the chart exercise, bar 5 has a $101.90 low. After bar 6 confirms it as a higher low, record that level. Bar 8 later closes at $101.50, below that already-known reference.

workshop.mistake: A sequence label is a description, not a probability of winning or a command to buy.

challenge.prompt: Highs rise from $101 to $104 but lows fall from $99 to $98. Is that a clean higher-high/higher-low sequence?
choices: Yes, because the last candle is green
challenge.explanation: The highs are higher but the lows are lower. Both lists must rise to describe higher highs and higher lows.

application.prompt: Write the reference before the next candle appears.
application.answer: Use the most recent already-confirmed higher low. Record its price and confirmation time. Do not choose a new low after seeing whether the trade wins.

title: Lower highs and lower lows
teach: A falling structure can make lower peaks and lower bottoms. A lower high says the rebound did not reach the prior peak. A lower low says price moved beneath the earlier bottom. Read the sequence rather than coloring one red candle as an entire downtrend. A strong rebound can invalidate the original idea.
example: Price falls from $105 to $102, rebounds to $104, then falls to $101. The rebound peak is lower and the new bottom is lower. A put idea still needs its own entry, contract and risk checks. Structure alone does not approve an order.
watch: A red candle can happen inside an uptrend. Structure compares swings, not colors alone.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes falling structure?
questions.explanation: A sequence of lower swing highs and lower swing lows describes falling structure.

workshop.goal: Describe falling structure and avoid treating every upward candle as a reversal.

steps.title: Read the highs and lows in order
steps.explain: A lower high peaks below the preceding confirmed high. A lower low falls below the preceding confirmed low. Together they describe downward structure over the chosen window.
steps.example: Highs $106 then $104; lows $102 then $100: both turn lists move downward. This is different from merely seeing one red candle.

steps.title: Distinguish a bounce from a break
steps.explain: A bounce can rise for several candles while remaining below the last confirmed lower high. The larger falling structure may still be intact. Define what would contradict it before watching the next candles.
steps.example: From $100, price bounces to $103 while the lower high is $104. That is upward movement, but it has not exceeded the recorded high.

steps.title: Mirror the interpretation, not every detail
steps.explain: For bearish trades, movement above a recorded lower high is adverse structure evidence. The exact threshold, timeframe and confirmation rule still matter. A stock rise does not map one-to-one to an option loss.
steps.example: A close above $104 can challenge the falling pattern. To price a put exit at that moment, you still need the exact option’s timestamped bid.

workshop.mistake: A put is purchased with a Buy action. Bearish direction does not mean the entry action is Sell.

application.prompt: Highs 110→108 and lows 106→104 are followed by a close 109. What should you investigate?

title: Break of structure without hindsight
teach: A structure break occurs when price crosses a level defined by the chosen swing rule. People use BOS and change of character in different ways, so a test needs an exact definition. Specify the level, candle timeframe, whether a close is required and when the swing was confirmed. A forming candle and a completed candle are different evidence.
example: A practice call uses a confirmed higher low of $101. A completed five-minute candle closes at $100.80. Under a close-below-$101 rule, that is a bearish break. A dip to $100.80 followed by a $101.20 close would not pass the same rule.
watch: A descriptive chart label is not automatically an enforced bot exit. Check the active policy.

questions.prompt: For a close-below-$101 rule, which qualifies?
choices: A prediction of the next close
questions.explanation: Only the completed close below the defined level satisfies that exact rule.

workshop.goal: State when a structure break becomes knowable and prevent hindsight from entering the decision.

steps.title: Freeze the reference first
steps.explain: A break of structure compares new price with an already identified swing level. CHoCH, or change of character, is commonly used for an initial break against the prior trend, but definitions vary. Specify the rule rather than rely on the acronym.
steps.example: Exercise rule: an upward sequence is challenged by a completed close below its latest confirmed higher low of $100.

steps.title: Wait only for the confirmation your rule requires
steps.explain: A real-time breach, one close and two closes are different tests. The confirmation time is when all required information is available. A chart may draw a marker at an earlier swing without making it tradable then.
steps.example: If the 5-minute candle ends 10:15 and first closes below $100, a one-close signal is knowable at 10:15 after receipt. Two-close confirmation waits for the next completed bar.

steps.title: Price the action after the signal
steps.explain: To test an exit, use a subsequent usable option quote and realistic costs. Do not sell at the best price earlier in the candle. Keep an unpriced signal separate from a completed hypothetical result.
steps.example: A 10:15 signal with the next valid bid at 10:15:02 must use that later observation under the test’s rules. A 10:14:30 bid was available before the signal existed.

workshop.mistake: The candle with the highest price is not automatically a bearish structure-change signal.

challenge.prompt: A rule requires two 5-minute closes below $100. They finish 10:15 and 10:20. When is confirmation first knowable?
challenge.explanation: The second required close does not exist until 10:20. Acting at 10:15 would test a different one-close rule.

application.prompt: The best bid occurred at 10:14 but confirmation came 10:20. Can the backtest use the 10:14 bid?
application.answer: No. Use an eligible quote after the actual confirmation time. Otherwise the test uses information and prices from incompatible moments.
