title: A breakout and its retest
teach: A breakout moves beyond a prior boundary. A retest comes back to that boundary. Some strategies wait to see whether it holds before entering; others use different rules. Waiting can avoid some false breaks but can also miss moves. The trade-off must be tested, not assumed.
example: An opening range ends at $102. Price closes at $102.30, revisits $102.05 and then closes higher. A retest strategy may regard the return as useful evidence. If it falls back and closes inside the range, the same strategy may reject it.
watch: The level must be known before the breakout. Do not redraw it to fit the trade.

questions.prompt: Why might a strategy wait for a retest?
choices: To see whether the old boundary holds
questions.explanation: A retest adds evidence about the boundary. It does not remove risk.

workshop.goal: Separate a breakout, a retest and a continuation, and handle a failed retest.

steps.title: Define the level before the breakout
steps.explain: Choose resistance from prior observations and state whether a close beyond it is required. A level drawn after the rally is not a fair test of the decision.
steps.example: Exercise resistance is $50. A completed close at $50.40 breaks above it under this example’s close-based rule.

steps.title: Observe the return to the area
steps.explain: A retest is a later return toward the broken level. Price may hold, cross or fail there. The return alone is not proof that resistance became support.
steps.example: Price drops from $50.80 toward $50.10. A later close at $50.50 offers different evidence from a close at $49.70.

steps.title: Specify the entry and invalidation separately
steps.explain: A retest strategy needs a trigger after the return and a condition that invalidates the idea. Waiting can improve clarity but may miss a move that never retests. Neither approach always wins.
steps.example: Example trigger: a completed candle closes back above the retest candle’s high. Example invalidation: a close below the recorded zone. These are exercises, not changes to CELO.

workshop.mistake: Do not label every pullback a successful retest. The outcome must still be observed.

challenge.prompt: Resistance $50 breaks, price returns and closes $49.70. What is the honest description?
choices: The return closed back below the level
challenge.explanation: The earlier breakout occurred, but the later close is below the level. Record both events rather than erase the failed follow-through.

application.prompt: What must be recorded before testing a retest entry?
application.answer: The prior resistance, breakout rule, retest zone, entry trigger and invalidation rule, each with the time it became known.

title: Failed breaks and recoveries
teach: A break can fail. Price may move below support, return above it and hold, or move above resistance and then fall back. A recovery strategy looks for a specified sequence. It should not call every bounce a recovery. The entry must be distinguishable from the falling move that came before it.
example: Support is $100. Price falls to $99.50, closes back at $100.20 and later stays above $100. A recovery rule might require those completed events. Buying at $99.50 before the reclaim would be a different rule.
watch: Describe the entry candle and required confirmation. Do not use the finished chart to move the entry earlier.

questions.prompt: Which comes before a confirmed reclaim entry?
choices: The required close back above support
questions.explanation: The specified reclaim must already have happened before its confirmation can justify an entry.

workshop.goal: Recognize a failed break without assuming the recovery guarantees a profitable reversal.

steps.title: Observe the break first
steps.explain: A failed break begins with price moving beyond a prior level. Decide what counts as a break and recovery using the same timestamp conventions. A wick and a close can tell different stories.
steps.example: Support $50 is crossed and a completed candle closes $49.60. Under the example rule, that is a downside break.

steps.title: Look for the recovery
steps.explain: A later close back above the level can show that sellers did not hold the break. It does not prove all sellers are finished. The recovery can itself fail.
steps.example: The next candle closes $50.20. That is a recovery above $50, not proof that price will reach $52.

steps.title: Connect the idea to a testable entry
steps.explain: Specify whether entry waits for recovery, a retest or another confirmation. Freeze the reference low before comparing results. Check the contract and account conditions separately from the chart.
steps.example: If entry requires the recovery close, the trade cannot enter at the earlier $49.60 low merely because it looks attractive later.

workshop.mistake: A failed downward break can suggest a bullish setup, but it does not automatically make a call cheap or liquid.

challenge.prompt: A recovery entry requires a close above $50. Low was $49.20 and later close $50.10. Which entry time is defensible?
choices: After the recovery close is known
At the earlier low using hindsight
challenge.explanation: The recovery condition becomes known only after the close. The earlier low cannot be selected with knowledge of the later recovery.

application.prompt: Price recovers $50 and then closes $49.80 again. What should the journal say?
application.answer: Recovery occurred, then failed to hold. Apply the written management rule and keep both observations in the record.

title: Two timeframes can disagree
teach: A one-minute chart describes small changes. An hourly chart groups many of them. Price can rally for a few minutes inside a broader decline. That is not necessarily bad data. Compare the same point in time, identify forming bars and say which timeframe your strategy uses for each decision.
example: At 10:12 the last one-minute candles are rising, but the last completed hourly candle was falling. The current hourly candle is not finished. A strategy may use hourly context and minute timing, but it must define how disagreement is handled.
watch: Indicators must use the candles and timestamps for their own timeframe. Never treat a forming hour as a completed one.

questions.prompt: Can rising one-minute candles occur inside a falling hourly trend?
choices: Only if the chart is broken
questions.explanation: Short moves can oppose the broader trend. Timeframe and confirmation timing matter.

workshop.goal: Write a precise account of conflicting timeframes instead of forcing a single direction.

steps.title: Name each timeframe’s job
steps.explain: A higher timeframe can provide context while a lower one times a setup. The role must be defined in advance. Do not keep changing which timeframe matters after a losing entry.
steps.example: The hour may describe a decline while the last five minutes show a bounce. Record both rather than calling the market simply bullish.

steps.title: Align the observation times
steps.explain: Compare completed bars available at the decision time. An hourly candle that closes later is future information. Session alignment and gaps also matter when building larger candles.
steps.example: At 10:20, a 9:30-to 10:30 hourly candle is still forming. Its final 10:30 close cannot be used to justify a 10:20 decision.

steps.title: Make conflict a rule, not a feeling
steps.explain: An entry policy may allow a countertrend setup or veto it. Protective exits may follow their own priorities. The lesson is to specify the behavior and test it, not to claim every timeframe must agree.
steps.example: A rule might block new bullish entries during a confirmed hourly decline. That does not imply it should delay an existing position’s protective exit.

workshop.mistake: Two timeframes disagreeing is not necessarily a data error. First check alignment, then interpret the different windows.

challenge.prompt: At 10:20, an hourly bar ends 10:30. Can its eventual bearish close be used in the 10:20 backtest?
choices: Yes, it is the same hour
No, that close was not available yet
challenge.explanation: The 10:30 close is future information at 10:20. Use the last completed bar or a clearly defined forming-bar rule.

application.prompt: Write the conflict without predicting an outcome.
application.answer: “Completed hourly structure is falling. Recent one-minute closes are rising within that decline. The entry policy decides whether this countertrend setup is allowed.”

title: Delta is an estimate
teach: Delta estimates how much an option price may change for a small $1 move in the underlying, with other inputs held still. A long call usually has positive delta; a long put usually has negative delta. Delta changes as conditions change. It is not a guaranteed payoff or a promise about the next dollar move.
example: A call has delta 0.40. A small $1 stock rise suggests about $0.40 more per option share if other factors stay still, or about $40 per standard contract. Actual quotes can differ because time, uncertainty and the spread change too.
watch: Use estimates to understand sensitivity, not to invent a missing executable quote.

questions.prompt: Delta 0.40 roughly estimates what for a $1 stock rise?
choices: $40 per standard contract, other inputs unchanged
questions.explanation: The estimated $0.40 option-share move is multiplied by 100 for a standard contract.

workshop.goal: Translate delta into a small-move estimate and explain its limits.

steps.title: Read the sign
steps.explain: Positive delta means a small stock rise tends to increase theoretical option value, all else fixed. Negative delta means the opposite. Purchased calls generally have positive delta and purchased puts negative delta.
steps.example: Call delta +0.40 suggests about +$0.40 premium for a $1 stock rise. Put delta −0.40 suggests about − $0.40 for the same rise.

steps.title: Scale to contracts
steps.explain: Delta is typically quoted per share of option premium. Multiply the estimated premium change by 100 and quantity for standard contracts. Keep the stock move’s sign in the calculation.
steps.example: A put with delta −0.40 and stock move − $0.50 has approximate premium change +$0.20. For 2 contracts, that is roughly +$40 before other effects.

steps.title: Recalculate as conditions change
steps.explain: Delta changes with price, time and volatility. It is a local sensitivity, not a fixed relationship over a large move. Use observed option quotes to determine actual sale results.
steps.example: Multiplying today’s delta by a $20 stock move can be misleading. The delta along that path is unlikely to remain unchanged.

workshop.mistake: Delta alone does not measure the chance of a profitable exit, because price paid, timing and costs matter.

challenge.explanation: 0.60 × $0.50 × 100 × 2 = about +$60. This is an estimate before other inputs and execution costs.

application.prompt: A put delta is −0.30 and stock rises $1. What is the direction of the estimated premium change?
application.answer: About − $0.30 per share, or − $30 per standard contract. The negative delta means a stock rise is adverse under the local estimate.

title: Gamma explains changing sensitivity
teach: Gamma describes how delta changes as the stock moves. Near expiration, some near-the-money options can become much more sensitive very quickly. A delta estimate made earlier can become outdated. This is one reason a fixed stock move does not imply the same option-dollar result throughout a trade.
example: A call’s delta is 0.40, then later 0.55. The next small stock move now has a different estimated effect. You cannot price the entire trade using the first delta as though it never changes.
watch: An option can become harder to manage even when the stock’s candles look similar.

questions.prompt: Why can the same stock move have a different option-price effect later?
questions.explanation: Gamma describes a changing delta. Time and volatility also affect the option.

workshop.goal: Explain why an option’s sensitivity can accelerate as the stock moves.

steps.title: Start with delta
steps.explain: Delta describes the current sensitivity to a small underlying move. Gamma describes how that sensitivity is estimated to change for a $1 underlying move. It is a change in delta, not a dollar profit by itself.
steps.example: Delta 0.40 and gamma 0.08 suggest delta might become about 0.48 after a $1 stock rise, holding other inputs fixed.

steps.title: Distinguish the first move from the next
steps.explain: When delta changes, the next similar stock move can affect the option differently. This is why a straight-line estimate can fail over a large path. Gamma itself can also change.
steps.example: The first small move might be described with delta near 0.40; a later move may use a higher delta. Do not assume each $1 rise always adds exactly $0.40.

steps.title: Understand why timing matters
steps.explain: Near expiration and near the strike, sensitivity can change rapidly. This can magnify both opportunity and management difficulty. A small premium does not mean a small or slow-changing risk.
steps.example: An option near its strike may react very differently before and after a sharp stock move. Refresh the quote rather than trusting an old Greek snapshot.

workshop.mistake: Gamma is not an extra guaranteed return to add to delta on every candle.

application.prompt: Why is using one delta for a large stock move unreliable?
application.answer: Because delta changes along the move, partly described by gamma. Time and volatility may also change, so a fresh option quote is needed.

title: Time can work against an option buyer
teach: Theta describes an estimated price change from time passing, with other inputs held still. Long options generally lose time value as expiration approaches. That does not mean every option falls by the same fixed amount each day. Price changes and uncertainty may overwhelm the time effect.
example: A stock stays near $100 while a call falls from $2.00 to $1.80. The lack of a favorable move and the loss of time value may be part of the reason. You still need quotes and context to explain the actual trade.
watch: Waiting is a decision. Your plan should say what you expect to happen and when you will reassess.

questions.prompt: Can a long option lose value while the stock barely moves?
questions.explanation: Time value and expected uncertainty can change even if the stock stays nearly still.

workshop.goal: Recognize time-value erosion without assuming a fixed daily charge.

steps.title: Separate intrinsic and remaining value
steps.explain: An option premium can contain intrinsic value plus value from remaining time and uncertainty. At expiration the extra time value is gone. Before then, market changes can increase or decrease the total premium.
steps.example: A call quoted $3 with $1 intrinsic value has $2 beyond intrinsic value. That $2 is not a guaranteed amount you can recover later.

steps.title: Interpret theta in units
steps.explain: Theta estimates the premium effect of a day passing with other inputs held fixed. A negative theta is common for purchased options. It is not a cash fee charged to your account and is not constant each day.
steps.example: Theta −0.04 suggests about − $4 per standard contract over a day in that model, before changes in stock price or volatility.

steps.title: Connect the clock to the trade thesis
steps.explain: If the expected move is slow or delayed, the option can lose value while waiting. A time-based exit may express a plan that the move should happen soon. Its usefulness must be tested rather than assumed.
steps.example: A stock stays flat for several days while a short-dated option gets cheaper. The entry direction was never disproved, but the timing may not fit the contract.

workshop.mistake: Do not multiply one theta reading by many days and call the result exact. Sensitivities and market prices change.

application.answer: Remaining time, implied volatility, spread and quote freshness. The record must support the explanation; theta alone cannot prove the exact cause.

title: Good news can still lose money
teach: An option price includes the market’s expectation of future movement. Before a major announcement that expectation may be high. After the event, uncertainty can fall. An option buyer can get the stock direction right and still lose if the move is too small or the option becomes cheaper for other reasons.
example: A call costs $4 before earnings. The stock rises a little after earnings but the call bid is $3.40. The correct direction did not cover what was priced into the option. This does not prove the feed is reversed.
watch: Separate what happened to the stock from what buyers would pay for the option.

questions.prompt: Can a call lose after the stock rises?
choices: Yes, other pricing factors can offset the rise
questions.explanation: A favorable stock move can be outweighed by falling time value or implied volatility.

workshop.goal: Understand how an expected announcement can be priced into an option before it happens.

steps.title: Distinguish news from expectations
steps.explain: Markets respond to what happened compared with what was expected. Good business news can coincide with a falling stock or option if buyers had already priced in a better outcome.
steps.example: A company reports growth, but less growth than investors expected. The headline sounds positive while the market reaction is negative.

steps.title: Consider uncertainty before and after
steps.explain: Before an event, options can reflect a wide range of possible outcomes. Once the event occurs, implied volatility may fall. That can reduce option premium even if the stock moves in your predicted direction.
steps.example: A call bought at $5 before an event might bid $4.50 after a small stock rise. Reduced uncertainty may contribute, but verify quotes and volatility data before assigning cause.

steps.title: Compare the actual contract path
steps.explain: Review entry premium, post-event bid, strike, expiration and spread. A correct forecast of the headline is not enough. The move must compensate for what the option cost and how it changed.
steps.example: Two contracts bought at $5 and sold at $4.50 lose $100 before fees. The result is determined by those prices, not by whether the headline was favorable.

workshop.mistake: An event-related volatility drop is a possible explanation, not something you can measure exactly from a stock chart alone.

application.prompt: What would make “good news caused a loss” a more useful review?
application.answer: State the expected outcome, actual stock reaction, option entry/exit prices and volatility/spread evidence. Separate observed facts from possible explanations.

title: Bid, ask and the price you can get
teach: The bid is what a buyer is currently offering. The ask is what a seller is requesting. Their difference is the spread. A midpoint is an estimate between them, not a guaranteed execution. Quotes have timestamps and sizes. A price from several minutes ago may be useless for a decision now.
example: Bid $1.90, ask $2.10. Buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses $20 per standard contract before fees. A $2.00 midpoint would hide half the spread on each side if treated as guaranteed.
watch: Use real quotes when available and clearly label hypothetical results. Do not count the spread twice.

questions.prompt: Buy at $2.10 and sell at $1.90. Gross result per standard contract?
questions.explanation: The 20-cent loss per option share is multiplied by 100.

workshop.goal: Price a hypothetical exit from the appropriate side of a fresh exact-contract quote.

steps.title: Use the selling side
steps.explain: A purchased option is sold to close. A current bid is a practical reference for a hypothetical sale, but it is not a broker-confirmed fill. The ask is what sellers request, not what buyers necessarily pay you.
steps.example: Bid $2.30, ask $2.50: valuing a sale at $2.50 assumes someone pays the ask. That is not established by the quote alone.

steps.title: Account for time and costs
steps.explain: Match the quote to the decision time, using the next eligible observation after the signal. Include fees and modeled slippage consistently. Do not reuse a quote from before the signal simply because it improves the result.
steps.example: A signal at 10:15:00 followed by a valid bid at 10:15:02 can support a hypothetical exit at that observation under the test rules. It still is not a fill.

steps.title: Label the result honestly
steps.explain: Separate live fills, paper broker fills and hypothetical quote-based results. Report missing sizes or timestamps. A calculated profit is useful only when the reader knows what evidence supports it.
steps.example: “Hypothetical +$30 using bid $2.30 after entry $2.00, before costs” is different from “Sold for +$30.” The latter requires execution evidence.

workshop.mistake: Never call an unfilled limit order or a midpoint valuation a completed profitable sale.

challenge.explanation: ($2.30 − $2.00) × 100 = +$30 hypothetically. The quote does not prove an order filled at that price.

application.prompt: If the only quote after the signal is crossed, what should you report?
application.answer: The signal time can be reported, but the priced result is unavailable until a valid quote is found under the test’s rules. Do not silently use the crossed price.

title: Liquidity includes size
teach: A bid does not promise that you can sell any quantity at that price. Its displayed size is part of the available evidence. Volume counts completed contracts over a period; open interest counts outstanding contracts. Neither guarantees an immediate fill for your order.
example: You hold eight contracts, but the best bid shows size two. A research test cannot honestly call eight contracts sold at that bid without an execution assumption. Some may fill at another price or wait.
watch: Price, size and timestamp belong together. A quote is not a fill.

questions.prompt: A bid size of two proves eight contracts can sell there:
questions.explanation: The visible size is smaller than the proposed sale. Larger execution is uncertain.

workshop.goal: Explain why a quoted price may not be available for your entire order.

steps.title: Read price and quantity together
steps.explain: The bid tells you a price buyers are displaying. Bid size tells you how many contracts are displayed there. Neither promises that the quote will remain available when your order arrives. A small spread alone does not prove there is enough size for your trade.
steps.example: You own 8 contracts. The best bid is $2.40 with size 3. That quote does not establish that all 8 can sell for $2.40.

steps.title: Walk through more than one price
steps.explain: An order can fill in pieces at different prices. Calculate proceeds from each piece, then divide by the total contracts to find the average price. Displayed depth is still only a snapshot, not a promise.
steps.example: If 3 sell at $2.40 and 5 sell at $2.35, proceeds are $720 + $1,175 = $1,895. The average is $2.36875 per share before costs.

steps.title: Distinguish activity from available buyers
steps.explain: Volume counts contracts traded during a period. Open interest counts outstanding contracts. Neither tells you exactly how many contracts you can sell right now. Check the current quote, size, age and actual fills.
steps.example: A contract can have high daily volume while its current bid size is only 1. Do not replace the size check with a popular-contract label.

workshop.mistake: A quote is an opportunity to attempt a trade, not proof of a completed trade.

title: Market and limit orders
teach: A market order seeks execution at available prices. It does not guarantee the last displayed price. A limit order sets the worst price you accept, but it may not fill. An order being accepted by the broker is not the same as it being completed.
example: You submit a sell limit of $2.10 while the bid is $2.00. It may wait. A market sell may execute sooner but at $2.00 or another available price. Your record must distinguish submitted, accepted, partially filled and filled.
watch: Check broker-confirmed quantity and price before declaring an exit complete.

questions.prompt: Which can remain unfilled even after submission?
questions.explanation: The market may never offer your limit price.

workshop.goal: Choose an order type by understanding what it controls and what it cannot promise.

steps.title: Separate urgency from price control
steps.explain: A market order asks for execution at available prices. A limit order sets a worst acceptable price, but may not fill. For selling, the limit is the minimum acceptable price. For buying, it is the maximum.
steps.example: The bid is $1.80 and ask is $2.00. A sell limit at $1.95 may wait. A market sell can fill near the available bid or worse if prices move.

steps.title: Understand what a stop becomes
steps.explain: A stop order generally becomes a market order when its trigger is reached. A stop-limit becomes a limit order. Triggering is not the same as filling. Brokers differ in supported option orders and trigger definitions.
steps.example: A sell stop at $1.80 cannot guarantee a $1.80 sale. If the market jumps to $1.60, a triggered market order may sell there. A $1.75 limit could remain unfilled.

steps.title: Confirm cancellation before replacement
steps.explain: An order can fill while a cancellation request is traveling. Read the final order status and remaining position before sending a replacement. Otherwise you can accidentally send more orders than intended.
steps.example: You ask to cancel a 4-contract order. Two contracts fill before cancellation completes. A replacement must account for those 2, not assume the original 4 are still available.

workshop.mistake: “Submitted,” “triggered,” “cancel requested” and “filled” describe different events.

title: Partial fills and odd quantities
teach: A partial fill means only some of the requested contracts traded. Position management must use what actually filled, not what was requested. Selling half also needs a rounding rule when the quantity is odd. The remaining quantity must never become negative or exceed the broker position.
example: You own five contracts. A plan that rounds half down requests two. If only one fills, four remain, and one of the first sale request is still outstanding. Resending two without checking can sell too much.
watch: Write a rounding rule before the trade and reconcile before retrying an order.

questions.prompt: Five held, one confirmed sold. How many remain?
questions.explanation: Only the filled contract is removed. Requested but unfilled quantities still need tracking.

workshop.goal: Reconcile partial sales without confusing an order request with your remaining position.

steps.title: Track requested, filled and remaining
steps.explain: A partial fill means only part of an order executed. Position size changes by the filled quantity, not the requested quantity. Keep the remaining open order separate from the remaining position.
steps.example: You own 10 and request a sale of 5. Only 2 fill. You still own 8, and 3 contracts remain on that order unless canceled or filled later.

steps.title: Make odd quantities explicit
steps.explain: You cannot sell half of a standard contract. A half-sale rule needs a stated rounding rule for odd quantities. Learn what your saved policy does rather than assuming all systems round the same way.
steps.example: Half of 5 is 2.5. A round-down policy sells 2 and leaves 3. A round-up policy sells 3 and leaves 2. This lesson changes neither choice.

steps.title: Add realized and unrealized results correctly
steps.explain: Profit on sold contracts is realized. The value of remaining contracts still changes. Count each filled contract once and keep fees attached to the actual executions.
steps.example: Buy 6 at $2. Sell 3 at $2.40: realized gross profit is $120. The other 3 marked at $1.80 have an unrealized $60 loss. Combined gross result at that mark is $60.

workshop.mistake: A planned half-sale is not a completed half-sale until the fills confirm it.

application.answer: First sale: +$100. Second sale: -$50. Total +$50 before fees, not +$200 from applying the first sale price to all 4.

title: A target and a trail do different jobs
teach: A profit target exits at a stated gain. A profit trail first records a peak, then exits after a specified amount is given back. A percentage of profit is not a percentage of the entire option price. Your plan must say whether it sells all contracts or only some.
example: Entry $2.00, peak bid $2.40. Peak profit is $40 per standard contract. Giving back 25% of that profit means giving back $10, so the reference trail is $2.30 before costs. A fast gap can execute below that reference.
watch: A trigger level is not a guaranteed fill price. Keep commissions and execution uncertainty in the calculation.

questions.prompt: Entry $2, peak $2.40, give back 25% of peak profit. Reference price?
questions.explanation: Peak profit is $0.40 per share. Retaining 75% leaves $0.30 above entry.

workshop.goal: Tell a fixed profit target from a trail that follows the highest profit reached.

steps.title: A target sells at a defined threshold
steps.explain: A fixed target says when to attempt a sale based on the gain from entry. It does not need a reversal first. The actual sale price depends on the order and available market.
steps.example: Entry $2. A 10% premium-gain target is $2.20. On 1 standard contract that is $20 gross profit if it sells at that price.

steps.title: A profit trail measures the retreat from a peak
steps.explain: Peak-profit giveback is a percentage of profit above entry, not a percentage of the entire option price. As a new peak is reached, the dollar threshold rises. The rule also needs a stated activation condition.
steps.example: Entry $2, peak $2.50: peak profit is $50 per contract. Giving back 20% means surrendering $10, so the threshold is $2.40.

steps.title: Combine stages without double counting
steps.explain: A staged rule can sell some contracts at a target and trail the remainder. Keep the quantities and prices separate. A tiny initial peak makes the first trailing distance tiny as well.
steps.example: Buy 4 at $2. Sell 2 at $2.20 for $40 gross profit. If the remaining 2 later sell at $2.40, they add $80. Total is $120 before fees.

workshop.mistake: A 20% giveback of profit is not a 20% drop in the option price.

title: Small gains still pay costs
teach: Gross profit is the price difference times quantity and multiplier. Net profit subtracts costs. A small gain can vanish after fees and execution costs. Separate commissions from spread and slippage so the same cost is not counted twice.
example: A standard contract bought for $2.00 and sold for $2.04 makes $4 gross. With a hypothetical $3.30 round-trip cost, net profit is $0.70. That $3.30 is a teaching assumption, not a universal broker fee.
watch: Never assume every positive percentage is a meaningful net gain.

questions.prompt: A $4 gross gain with $3.30 total costs leaves:
questions.explanation: Subtract total costs from the gross gain.

workshop.goal: Calculate whether a small gross gain survives the costs of trading.

steps.title: Start with actual purchase and sale prices
steps.explain: Subtract the entry price from the exit price, multiply by 100 for a standard contract, then multiply by quantity. This gives gross trading profit before fees.
steps.example: Buy at $2.00 and sell at $2.04:4 cents × 100 = $4 gross profit per contract. A 2% gain does not mean $2 profit.

steps.title: Subtract costs once
steps.explain: If you already use the actual ask paid and bid received, the spread is already reflected in that difference. Add actual fees, or explicit modeled fees and slippage for a simulation. Do not subtract the spread twice.
steps.example: An illustrative $4 gain minus $1.30 round-trip fees and $2 modeled slippage leaves $0.70. Those are example costs, not a promise about your broker.

steps.title: Include losses in the same comparison
steps.explain: A system with many small wins can still lose money if occasional losses are larger. Apply costs consistently to wins and losses, including partial sales.
steps.example: Four gross $4 wins and one gross $20 loss total -$4 before costs. At $3.30 modeled costs per trade, the five-trade net becomes -$20.50.

workshop.mistake: Gross profit, after-fee profit and a hypothetical after-cost estimate are different numbers.

application.answer: No. That price difference already contains the spread. Separately account for fees and any additional modeled slippage without counting the same cost twice.

title: Size from a real risk assumption
teach: A risk budget is the amount you plan to risk on a trade. For a premium stop, planned per-contract loss is entry premium minus stop premium, times the contract multiplier. Divide the budget by that loss and round down. This estimate only makes sense if the stop is actually monitored, and it does not cap a gap loss.
example: Account $10,000, risk budget 1% = $100. Entry $2.00, stop $1.60 gives $40 planned loss per standard contract. Two contracts risk $80 before costs; three would exceed the budget. Costs and uncertainty can reduce the allowed size further.
watch: A line on a chart is not automatically an enforceable stop. Never size from a reference-only line as though it guarantees protection.

questions.prompt: Before costs, how many $40-risk contracts fit a $100 budget?
questions.explanation: Round down: $100 divided by $40 is 2.5, so two fit the planned budget.

workshop.goal: Size a trade using a loss assumption you can actually defend.

steps.title: Choose the risk assumption before quantity
steps.explain: For a purchased option, the full premium plus costs is a conservative loss basis. A smaller planned-stop loss is only an estimate and depends on monitoring, execution and gaps. A reference line alone is not an enforced stop.
steps.example: At $2 premium and $1.30 example round-trip fees, full-cost risk is $201.30 per standard contract. A chart line does not automatically reduce that to $20.

steps.title: Calculate both budget limits
steps.explain: Divide the allowed risk budget by risk per contract and round down. Separately check purchase-cost limits and available buying power. Use the smallest permitted quantity, not whichever calculation gives more contracts.
steps.example: A $10,000 account with a 5% example risk budget allows $500. $500 ÷ $201.30 permits 2 contracts. A $300 purchase cap would reduce that to 1.

steps.title: Recalculate when the contract changes
steps.explain: A new premium, multiplier, fee schedule or account balance changes the calculation. Do not reuse a quantity from a cheaper contract. Zero contracts is a valid result when one contract exceeds the limit.
steps.example: A $100 budget cannot buy a $150 standard option plus fees under a full-cost cap. Rounding up to 1 would exceed the budget.

workshop.mistake: A percentage setting is not a contract count. The contract cost and enforceable risk assumption matter.

title: Several trades can share one risk
teach: Separate tickers do not always mean separate risks. Broad-market funds and large technology stocks can move together. If several positions all need the same market rise, their losses may arrive together. Evaluate total open exposure, not just each ticket in isolation.
example: Three calls each have a planned $100 risk. A broad selloff can hurt all three, creating at least $300 of planned risk before gaps and costs. Different ticker names do not cancel that exposure.
watch: A per-trade budget and an account-wide limit answer different questions.

questions.prompt: Three correlated $100-risk positions may create:
questions.explanation: Separate positions can lose at the same time.

workshop.goal: Recognize when different positions depend on the same market move.

steps.title: Count shared exposure, not just ticker names
steps.explain: Different tickers can move together because they share a sector, index or economic driver. Several bullish positions can all lose during the same broad decline. Separate tickets do not guarantee separate risks.
steps.example: Calls on three large technology companies may all suffer when the technology sector drops. Owning three names is not automatically three independent bets.

steps.title: Add the dollars at risk
steps.explain: Look at total committed premium and the loss assumptions across open positions. A per-trade limit can be respected while the combined account exposure is still large.
steps.example: Three purchased-option positions each cost $600. Together they commit $1,800 before costs. On a $10,000 account, that is 18% of the account.

steps.title: Review the combined scenario
steps.explain: Ask what happens if the shared reason for the trades fails. Avoid assuming that one position must offset another unless its exposure and size actually support that claim.
steps.example: A tiny put position does not necessarily balance several large call positions. Write down the scenario and dollar exposure instead of calling it hedged by appearance.

workshop.mistake: More tickers can still mean more of the same risk.

title: Exercise and assignment
teach: Exercise is using the right in an option. Assignment is the obligation received by an option seller. Standard equity calls generally involve buying or delivering shares; puts involve selling or buying shares. Many equity options can be exercised before expiration. The broker’s rules and available funds matter.
example: Exercising one standard $100 equity call normally requires paying $10,000 for 100 shares. That is different from selling the option itself. A short option may be assigned before you expect, so do not treat expiration as the only possible event.
watch: Know the contract’s exercise style and settlement rules. Check your broker’s deadlines instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: Exercising a standard $100 equity call usually requires:
questions.explanation: The strike is per share, normally for 100 shares on a standard equity contract.

workshop.goal: Distinguish selling an option from using its right or meeting a seller’s obligation.

steps.title: The buyer has a right
steps.explain: Exercise uses the contract right. For a standard physically settled stock call, the holder buys 100 shares at the strike. For a put, the holder sells 100 shares at the strike. Product terms can differ.
steps.example: One $50 stock call exercised means buying 100 shares for $5,000, not merely paying the option premium again. The account needs to handle that stock transaction.

steps.title: The seller can receive an obligation
steps.explain: Assignment is the seller’s side of exercise. A short call can require delivery of shares; a short put can require buying shares. American-style options can be exercised before expiration, so obligations are not limited to the final day.
steps.example: A short $50 put assigned on a standard contract generally requires buying 100 shares for $5,000. Premium received does not remove that obligation.

steps.title: Compare closing with exercising
steps.explain: Selling to close transfers the option and ends that long option position after it fills. Exercising may sacrifice remaining time value and create stock exposure. Check your broker’s rules and the exact product rather than assuming exercise is the normal way to exit.
steps.example: A call with $3 intrinsic value and a $3.40 sale value has 40 cents of additional value. Exercising captures the intrinsic economics but can forfeit that extra value.

workshop.mistake: A long option position and a short option obligation are not interchangeable.

challenge.prompt: One standard $60 call is exercised. What stock purchase does that represent?
challenge.explanation: The standard multiplier is 100. Exercise at a $60 strike means $6,000 of stock purchase, subject to the product and broker rules.

application.prompt: You sell your long option to close and the order fills. Is that the same as exercising?
application.answer: No. You sold the contract. Exercising uses the right to transact in the underlying under the contract terms.

title: Do not drift into expiration
teach: As expiration approaches, a small stock move can change an option’s outcome quickly. Some contracts settle in shares and others in cash. Broker exercise deadlines may be earlier than you expect. An in-the-money expiration can create a stock position or an obligation, depending on the contract and your side.
example: A learner plans to close before expiration but forgets. The option finishing in the money may lead to exercise or assignment under broker procedures. A small-looking option position can create a much larger share exposure.
watch: For paper practice, write an exit deadline and verify the position is closed. Never rely on an unverified assumption about automatic handling.

questions.prompt: Which is safest to verify before holding near expiration?
choices: Settlement type and broker exercise deadlines
questions.explanation: Expiration handling can change the type and size of your exposure.

workshop.goal: Plan an exit before expiration creates obligations you did not intend.

steps.title: Expiration is a deadline, not an exit plan
steps.explain: An option can lose remaining time value quickly as expiration approaches. In-the-money positions may be exercised under broker and clearing procedures. Do not assume doing nothing means a harmless automatic close.
steps.example: A long stock call that finishes in the money may lead to stock ownership if exercised. That is different from the cash result of selling the option earlier.

steps.title: Check the broker’s actual cutoff
steps.explain: Trading hours, exercise instructions, automatic-exercise handling and risk liquidation can differ by product and broker. Some contracts settle in cash; others deliver shares. Learn those terms before the final session.
steps.example: Your review should identify the exact contract, last trading time, instruction deadline and settlement method. A generic “options expire Friday” reminder is not enough.

steps.title: Verify the position after the deadline
steps.explain: A closing order that never filled does not remove the position. Review fills, account holdings and any resulting stock or cash settlement. Do not rely only on an order-submitted notification.
steps.example: A sell limit remains open at the close. The option was not sold. You still need to check the broker’s expiration treatment and the resulting account position.

workshop.mistake: An unfilled closing order is not protection from expiration handling.

title: Understand a debit call spread
teach: A debit call spread buys a lower-strike call and sells a higher-strike call on the same underlying and expiration. The sold call reduces the initial cost but caps the upside. The textbook payoff assumes the spread remains intact. Early assignment, execution and closing one leg can change the real exposure.
example: Buy a $100 call for $4 and sell a $105 call for $1. Net debit is $3, normally $300. At expiration, the intact spread’s maximum value is $5, so maximum profit is $200 before costs, and maximum loss of the debit is $300 under the payoff assumptions.
watch: Learn the obligations of the short leg before considering multi-leg strategies. This lesson does not enable spread trading in CELO.

questions.prompt: A $5-wide spread costs $3. Its maximum expiration profit before costs is:
questions.explanation: Width minus debit is $2 per share, normally $200.

workshop.goal: Calculate the cost, maximum profit and maximum loss of a simple debit call spread.

steps.title: Build the two legs
steps.explain: A bull call debit spread buys a lower-strike call and sells a higher-strike call on the same underlying with the same expiration and equal quantities. The short call reduces the purchase cost but caps the expiration upside.
steps.example: Buy a $50 call for $4 and sell a $55 call for $1. Net debit is $3 per share, or $300 for one standard spread before fees.

steps.title: Work out the expiration boundaries
steps.explain: For this example, maximum expiration loss is the $300 debit. Maximum expiration profit is strike width minus debit: ($5 - $3) × 100 = $200. Breakeven is lower strike plus debit: $53.
steps.example: At expiration with stock $52, the long call is worth $2 and the short call $0. The spread is worth $200, so the $300 purchase has a $100 loss before costs.

steps.title: Respect the two-leg execution risk
steps.explain: The neat payoff assumes the matched spread is maintained and settlement handled correctly. Early assignment of the short leg, closing one leg alone, fees and execution prices can complicate the account result.
steps.example: Selling the long call while leaving the short call open removes the original protection. Do not treat the remaining short option as if it still has the spread’s capped risk.

workshop.mistake: The maximum-profit formula is an expiration payoff for the matched position, not a guaranteed sale price today.

challenge.prompt: A $5-wide debit spread costs $2. What is maximum expiration profit for one standard spread before costs?
challenge.explanation: Width $5 minus debit $2 = $3 per share, or $300. Maximum loss is the $200 debit.

application.prompt: For the $50/$55 spread costing $3, calculate expiration P&L at stock $50, $53 and $57.
application.answer: At $50: -$300. At $53: $0. At $57: +$200. Above $55 the two calls offset additional stock gains, so profit is capped.

title: Covered does not mean protected
teach: A covered call combines shares with a call sold against them. The premium can offset some loss, but the stock can still fall sharply. The sold call can limit the gain if the stock rises beyond the strike. Cash-secured puts also carry meaningful stock downside if assigned.
example: Own 100 shares at $50 and receive $100 for selling a call. If the shares fall to $40, the $1,000 stock loss is only partly offset by the $100 premium. Ignoring other effects, that is still a $900 loss before fees.
watch: Receiving premium is not free income. It comes with obligations and downside.

questions.prompt: Does a covered call remove stock downside?
questions.explanation: The premium is limited while the shares can fall much further.

workshop.goal: Explain the protection a covered call provides and the stock risk it leaves behind.

steps.title: Identify what covers the call
steps.explain: A covered call holds enough shares to deliver against the short call. For a standard contract, that is usually 100 shares for each call sold. Covered describes the delivery obligation, not protection from a stock decline.
steps.example: Buy 100 shares at $50 and sell a $55 call for $2. You receive $200 premium, but you still own $5,000 of stock exposure.

steps.title: Calculate the downside honestly
steps.explain: Premium received reduces the effective cost, but most stock downside remains. In this example, stock dropping to $40 at expiration loses $1,000 on shares, partly offset by $200 premium.
steps.example: Combined result is -$800 before costs. Calling the trade covered does not turn that loss into a small fixed amount.

steps.title: Recognize the capped upside
steps.explain: If shares are delivered at the $55 strike, the stock gain is $500 plus $200 premium, for $700 before costs. A much larger stock rise does not add the same upside while the short call remains. Assignment can also occur early.
steps.example: At stock $65 at expiration, the matched covered call still has roughly the $700 capped payoff in this example, rather than the $1,500 gain from simply holding the shares.

workshop.mistake: Covered calls exchange some upside for premium; they do not eliminate stock risk.

application.answer: $48 per share: $50 stock cost minus $2 premium. Below that, the combined position loses money despite being covered.

title: Win rate is not profitability
teach: Win rate counts how often trades win. Profitability also depends on how large wins and losses are and on costs. A strategy can win frequently yet lose money. Review both typical outcomes and unusually large losses rather than chasing the prettiest percentage.
example: Eight wins of $10 make $80. Two losses of $60 lose $120. The strategy wins 80% of the time but loses $40 before costs. Increasing the number of small wins alone does not solve the large losses.
watch: Ask how much is won, how much is lost and how many observations support the result.

questions.prompt: Eight $10 wins and two $60 losses total:
questions.explanation: $80 minus $120 is a $40 loss.

workshop.goal: Judge results using both win size and loss size instead of win rate alone.

steps.title: Count outcomes first
steps.explain: Win rate is winning trades divided by all completed trades in the group. It says how often trades won, not how much they won. Keep the definition of a win consistent, preferably after the costs used in the report.
steps.example: Eight wins out of ten is 80%. That sounds strong, but the dollar sizes still decide the final result.

steps.title: Add dollars, then compare
steps.explain: Average win and average loss show whether small wins can pay for larger losses. Profit factor divides total winning dollars by the absolute total losing dollars. With no losses it is undefined or shown as no losses, not proof of unlimited quality.
steps.example: Eight $10 wins total $80. Two $60 losses total $120. Net is -$40 and profit factor is $80 ÷ $120 = 0.67 before any additional costs.

steps.title: Look beyond a short streak
steps.explain: A few trades can produce unstable statistics. Review different sessions and conditions and keep individual strategies, versions and account modes identifiable. A striking percentage from two trades is weak evidence.
steps.example: Two wins out of two produce 100% win rate, but reveal little about rare losses. More completed observations are needed to understand the pattern.

workshop.mistake: A high win rate can coexist with a losing account.

challenge.prompt: Six wins of $20 and four losses of $40. Total result before costs?
challenge.explanation: Wins total $120 and losses $160. Net is -$40 despite a 60% win rate.

application.prompt: Three wins total $300 and two losses total $150. Find net profit and profit factor.
application.answer: Net is $150. Profit factor is $300 ÷ $150 = 2.0. Both need the trade count, period and cost basis to be meaningful.

title: Drawdown and recovery
teach: Drawdown is the decline from a prior equity peak. A later recovery does not erase the stress or risk of that decline. Percent losses and recovery gains use different starting balances. A strategy’s final profit can hide a painful path.
example: An account falls from $10,000 to $8,000, a 20% drawdown. To return from $8,000 to $10,000, it needs $2,000, or a 25% gain. That is why limiting loss size matters even when a strategy later recovers.
watch: Review the path of results, not just the last total.

questions.prompt: After a 20% drop from $10,000, the gain needed to recover is:
questions.explanation: $2,000 divided by the remaining $8,000 is 25%.

workshop.goal: Measure a drop from an account peak and understand the recovery required.

steps.title: Measure from the previous peak
steps.explain: Drawdown is the decline from a prior high to a later low in the chosen account or strategy value series. It is different from one trade’s loss or the change since the start of today.
steps.example: A series rises from $10,000 to $12,000, then falls to $9,000. The drawdown from the $12,000 peak is $3,000, or 25%.

steps.title: Recovery uses a smaller starting base
steps.explain: After a loss, the same percentage gain does not restore the original amount. Calculate recovery from the reduced balance. Larger drawdowns demand disproportionately larger percentage gains.
steps.example: From $9,000 back to $12,000 requires $3,000 ÷ $9,000 = 33.3%. A 25% gain from $9,000 reaches only $11,250.

steps.title: Use a consistent series
steps.explain: Closed-trade equity and account equity including open positions can show different drawdowns. Deposits and withdrawals also affect the account. Label the series and do not mix them without adjustment.
steps.example: An open position may be down $500 while the closed-trade curve is flat. That does not mean the account experienced no drawdown.

workshop.mistake: A recovery percentage must use the balance after the loss as its denominator.

challenge.prompt: An account falls from $10,000 to $8,000. What gain returns it to $10,000?
challenge.explanation: It needs $2,000 on an $8,000 base: 25%.

application.prompt: A sequence is $10,000, $10,500, $9,500, $10,200. What is the largest peak-to-trough dollar drop?
application.answer: $1,000, from $10,500 to $9,500. The later $10,200 recovery does not erase the earlier drawdown.

title: A fair test uses the same trades
teach: To compare exits, hold the entries, option contracts and quantities fixed. Only the intended exit difference should change. Use information available at the decision time. Missing quotes make a result uncertain; they are not permission to insert the day’s best price. A rule chosen after seeing a trade is unproven until tested on new evidence.
example: Exit A uses ten trades and exit B uses only the three with available winning quotes. Comparing their totals is unfair. Compare matched trades, state the exclusions and keep a fresh period that was not used to choose the rule.
watch: Hypothetical bids are not broker-confirmed fills. Keep paper, live and simulated results separate.

questions.prompt: What makes an exit comparison fair?
choices: Same entries and contracts, honest costs and matched data
questions.explanation: Matching the inputs helps isolate the effect of the exit rule.

workshop.goal: Compare exit rules fairly without changing the trades underneath the comparison.

steps.title: Hold the entry fixed
steps.explain: To study an exit, use the same entry time, contract, entry price and quantity for both rules. Change only the exit being tested. Otherwise a better result may come from easier entries or different contracts.
steps.example: Rule A and rule B both start with the same 2 contracts at $3. One sells earlier. Comparing that with a different strike bought for $1 does not isolate the exit.

steps.title: Use information available at the decision
steps.explain: A signal cannot act before it becomes knowable. Price the hypothetical sale using eligible subsequent quotes and explicit costs. Missing quote data is a limitation, not a zero-dollar outcome or permission to invent a price.
steps.example: A candle closes at 10:15. A bid from 10:14 cannot price that close-based signal. Use the next valid observation allowed by the test, and label it hypothetical.

steps.title: Reserve newer trades for confirmation
steps.explain: Trying many rules increases the chance that one looks good by luck. Record every variant, freeze the selected rule and test it on newer unseen trades. Report missing comparisons and uncertainty instead of only the best-looking total.
steps.example: If you pick a threshold because it saved yesterday’s loss, yesterday is fitting evidence. A fresh group of trades is needed before claiming the rule repeats.

workshop.mistake: An attractive backtest is not the same as a proven improvement or a broker fill.

challenge.prompt: Candidate profit is $80 on trade A and baseline profit is $50 on that same trade. Paired difference?
challenge.explanation: $80 - $50 = +$30. Repeat this subtraction for each identical eligible trade.

application.prompt: Three trades have baseline results $20, -$40, $30. Candidate results are $10, -$20, missing. What can you compare?
application.answer: Use the same first two trades: baseline -$20, candidate -$10, paired improvement +$10. Report the third as missing. Do not compare the candidate’s two trades with all three baseline trades.

title: Build your own paper review
teach: Write the setup, entry trigger, contract, quantity, invalidation, exit plan and cost assumptions before a pretend trade. Afterwards compare the plan with what actually happened. Separate a bad setup from poor execution or an exit that did not follow its rule. A losing trade can follow a reasonable plan; one winner can come from a poor process.
example: Your review says: I expected a reclaim of $100; entered after the close at $100.20; planned to reassess below $99.80; used two standard contracts. Then list the actual times, bid and ask, fills if any, costs and the reason for exit. Mark unavailable facts as missing.
watch: The final goal is to explain a decision clearly, including what you do not know. Use paper practice and review before risking money.

questions.prompt: A useful review should compare:
choices: The written plan with the recorded decisions and execution
Your result with a hindsight peak
questions.explanation: The comparison shows whether the problem was the idea, the execution, the exit or missing evidence.

workshop.goal: Build a review that explains the decision, the execution and the lesson separately.

steps.title: Record the plan before seeing the outcome
steps.explain: Write the setup, exact contract, entry trigger, invalidation, sizing basis and intended exit. Record what information was known then. This lets you distinguish following a bad plan from failing to follow a reasonable plan.
steps.example: Example plan: buy 2 standard calls at a maximum $2 premium after a completed range breakout. Record the actual range and confirmation time rather than writing “looked bullish” afterward.

steps.title: Reconcile what actually happened
steps.explain: Compare requested orders with confirmed fills. Calculate each sale separately, subtract known fees and identify missing information. Include why the trade ended and whether that reason matched the entry-time plan.
steps.example: Buy 2 at $2. Sell 1 at $2.30 and 1 at $1.90: +$30 - $10 = +$20 gross. With $2.60 total example fees, net is $17.40.

steps.title: Choose one next experiment
steps.explain: Separate observations from explanations you have not proved. A profitable outcome can come from poor process and a loss can occur despite following the plan. Choose one specific improvement to test rather than rewriting everything from one trade.
steps.example: Observation: the second sale occurred later than planned. Next test: verify whether the decision was delayed or the order waited for a fill. Do not immediately assume a tighter stop fixes both.

workshop.mistake: A useful review explains what was known, what was done and what is still uncertain.

challenge.prompt: A trade lost money but followed its recorded plan. What does that prove?
choices: Only that this outcome lost; more evidence is needed about the rule
challenge.explanation: One loss does not establish the cause or the long-run quality. Check the entry, execution, exit and costs against the recorded plan.

application.prompt: Write a five-line review for the example: entry, first sale, second sale, net result and one next question.
application.answer: Entry: 2 at $2. First sale: 1 at $2.30. Second sale: 1 at $1.90. Net: $17.40 after $2.60 example fees. Next question: did both sale decisions and fills follow the recorded plan?
